title: The Bystander Effect: Why People Don't Help
passage: Today we're going to talk about a phenomenon that's been studied extensively in social psychology: the bystander effect. Now, the classic example is the Kitty Genovese case in 1964. Reports at the time claimed that 38 witnesses watched her murder and did nothing. But actually, later research showed those numbers were exaggerated. Still, the case sparked decades of research. So what is the bystander effect? It's the finding that individuals are less likely to help someone in need when other people are present. Why does this happen? Two main factors: diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance. Diffusion of responsibility means that when multiple people are around, each person feels less personally responsible. Pluralistic ignorance is when people look to others to figure out how to act. If no one else looks concerned, you might think there's no emergency. In one famous experiment, researchers filled a room with smoke. When participants were alone, they reported it quickly. But when with two other calm confederates, most didn't report it at all. So, the takeaway is that the presence of others can actually inhibit helping behavior. But recent studies show that in clear, dangerous emergencies, the effect weakens. And being in a good mood or having prior experience can also make people more likely to intervene.

title: The Disappearance of the Roanoke Colony
passage: Professor: Today we're going to discuss one of the most enduring mysteries in American history: the lost colony of Roanoke. In 1587, a group of about 115 English settlers established a colony on Roanoke Island, off the coast of what is now North Carolina. Their leader, John White, sailed back to England for supplies, but due to the Spanish Armada, he couldn't return for three years. When he finally did, in 1590, the colony was gone. The only clues were the word 'CROATOAN' carved into a post and the letters 'CRO' on a tree. The settlers' houses had been dismantled, which suggests they left intentionally, not attacked. White had told them to carve a cross if they were forced to leave, but there was no cross. So where did they go? Many historians believe they integrated with the Croatoan people, a Native American tribe on nearby Hatteras Island. Recent archaeological evidence, like a 16th-century gold ring and a slate with a secret symbol, supports this theory. But others argue they moved inland and were assimilated by other tribes. What's clear is that the word 'Croatoan' was not a distress signal but a destination. The mystery remains, but it's likely the settlers simply relocated and adapted to a new life.

title: The Evolution of Impressionist Brushwork
passage: Okay, let's pick up where we left off. Last time we talked about the subject matter of Impressionist paintings—how they captured modern life. But today I want to focus on something more technical: the brushwork itself. Now, you might think a brushstroke is just a brushstroke, but for the Impressionists, it became a revolutionary tool. Before them, academic painting prized smooth, invisible brushwork. You weren't supposed to see how the paint got on the canvas. But artists like Monet, Renoir, and Pissarro did the opposite. They used short, broken, and often thick strokes of pure color. Why? Because they were trying to capture the fleeting effects of light and atmosphere. If you look at Monet's series of haystacks, for example, the strokes don't blend into a smooth surface. Instead, they sit side by side. From a distance, your eye mixes those colors optically, creating a vibrant, shimmering effect. This technique—called optical mixing—was a radical departure. It meant the viewer's eye became an active participant in completing the painting. Now, this wasn't just a stylistic choice. It was also made possible by new technology: the invention of the metal paint tube in 1841. Before that, artists had to mix their own paints in the studio. The tube allowed them to paint outdoors, en plein air, and work quickly to catch the changing light. So you see, the brushwork wasn't just about style; it was about a whole new way of seeing and painting.

title: The Gesture-Speech Connection in Language Development
passage:
Today, I want to talk about a common misconception in language development. Many people assume that language acquisition is purely about words—vocabulary, grammar, syntax. But research shows that gestures, especially hand movements, play a crucial role.

Take, for instance, a study with toddlers. Researchers observed children between 14 and 18 months. They found that the number of gestures a child used predicted their later vocabulary size better than the number of words they spoke at that age. In other words, a child who points, waves, or reaches more is likely to develop a richer vocabulary later on.

But it's not just about children. Even adults gesture when they speak, often unconsciously. And these gestures aren't just random. They coordinate with speech in precise ways. For example, when we explain a spatial concept—like how to get to the library—our hands trace the path. This helps both the speaker and the listener process the information.

So, what does this mean for language learning? Some educators now incorporate gestures into teaching. For example, when teaching a new word like 'under', a teacher might physically place a hand under a table. Students who see and mimic these gestures remember the word better. This suggests that language is not just in the mind, but in the body as well.

title: The Mystery of the Plain of Jars
passage:
Okay, so today we're going to talk about one of the most intriguing archaeological mysteries in Southeast Asia – the Plain of Jars in Laos. Located on a plateau in central Laos, this site contains thousands of stone jars, some weighing up to ten tons. They're scattered across hundreds of square kilometers. Now, the obvious question is: what were they used for? 

Early researchers in the 1930s assumed they were funerary urns, because they found human remains and pottery nearby. But that interpretation was later challenged. In the 1970s, a new hypothesis emerged: the jars might have been used to store water or rice wine. However, no residue of either has ever been found inside them. 

More recently, in 2016, a team from the Australian National University conducted a detailed survey. They discovered that the jars were quarried from sandstone and granite sources up to 10 kilometers away. That's a huge logistical effort. And they also found that the jars were deliberately placed along a ancient trade route. So now many archaeologists think the jars served a dual purpose: they marked territory and were used in burial rituals. But the debate is far from over. 

What's really fascinating is that local legends claim the jars were made by a giant king to store his rice wine. So you see, even today, we're not entirely sure.

title: The Role of Sea Otters in Kelp Forest Ecosystems
passage:
Professor: Today we're going to discuss a classic example of a trophic cascade, and that's the relationship between sea otters, sea urchins, and kelp forests. Now, kelp forests are incredibly productive ecosystems, providing habitat and food for numerous marine species. But they're also vulnerable to overgrazing by sea urchins. Sea urchins feed on kelp, and if their populations explode, they can turn a lush kelp forest into a barren wasteland—what we call an urchin barren.

So what keeps sea urchins in check? That's where sea otters come in. Sea otters are voracious predators of sea urchins. They consume large numbers of them, and by doing so, they protect the kelp forest. This is a textbook example of a top-down effect, where a predator controls the abundance of its prey, which in turn benefits the primary producer.

Now, here's an interesting twist. In the 18th and 19th centuries, sea otters were hunted nearly to extinction for their fur. As a result, sea urchin populations skyrocketed, and many kelp forests along the Pacific coast collapsed. When sea otters were reintroduced or protected in certain areas, the kelp forests began to recover. This shows just how crucial a single species can be to an entire ecosystem.

But it's not always that simple. Recent studies suggest that in some regions, factors like disease and warming ocean temperatures also affect kelp health. So while sea otters are important, they're not the only piece of the puzzle. Next time, we'll look at another example of a trophic cascade involving wolves in Yellowstone.

title: The Mystery of the Bermuda Triangle: Methane Hydrates
passage:
Professor: Today we're going to talk about the Bermuda Triangle, a region in the western part of the North Atlantic Ocean where a number of aircraft and ships are said to have disappeared under mysterious circumstances. Now, many of you have probably heard of this. But what I want to focus on today is not the paranormal explanations, but a scientific hypothesis that has gained some traction: methane hydrates.

So what are methane hydrates? They're ice-like structures that form when methane gas is trapped in water molecules under high pressure and low temperature. These hydrates are stable in the deep ocean, but if the pressure decreases or the temperature increases, the methane can be released rapidly. And when methane is released, it can cause the water to become less dense, which could theoretically cause a ship to sink. Also, if a large amount of methane bubbles up to the surface, it could reduce the density of the air, causing aircraft to lose lift.

Now, this hypothesis was proposed by a few scientists, but it's not without criticism. Some argue that the required conditions for such a massive release are rare and that there's no direct evidence linking methane hydrates to any specific disappearance. Nevertheless, it's an interesting example of how natural phenomena can be used to explain seemingly supernatural events. Next time, we'll look at another scientific explanation for the Bermuda Triangle involving rogue waves.

title: The Evolution of the Skyscraper: From Masonry to Steel
passage: Professor: Today we'll explore how skyscrapers became possible. Before the late 19th century, buildings were limited to about 10 or 12 stories because walls had to support their own weight. The taller the building, the thicker the walls needed to be. So, what changed? Two key inventions: the elevator and structural steel. The elevator, perfected by Elisha Otis in the 1850s, made upper floors desirable. But the real breakthrough was the steel skeleton frame, first used in the Home Insurance Building in Chicago in 1885. Instead of relying on thick masonry walls, architects could hang the exterior on a steel frame. This allowed buildings to soar. However, early skyscrapers faced a problem: wind. Tall, lightweight structures swayed. So engineers developed diagonal bracing and later, tuned mass dampers. For example, the Taipei 101 uses a 660-ton steel pendulum to reduce sway. So you see, skyscrapers aren't just about height; they're a balance of technology, safety, and comfort.

title: The Birth of Opera: Camerata's Experiment
passage: Okay, so today we're going to talk about the birth of opera around the year 1600 in Italy. Now, you might think opera was invented to be popular entertainment, but actually it started as an experiment by a group of intellectuals in Florence called the Camerata. They were aristocrats, poets, and musicians who met regularly to discuss art and science. Their big idea was to recreate what they believed ancient Greek drama must have sounded like. They thought that in Greek plays, every word was sung, not spoken. So they set out to create a new kind of music where the text reigned supreme. The result was a style called monody—a single vocal line with simple instrumental accompaniment, so the words could be clearly understood. The first operas were mostly private performances for the nobility, not public. For example, Jacopo Peri's 'Dafne' in 1598 is often called the first opera, but it was performed at a small gathering. The Camerata wasn't trying to write hit tunes; they were trying to revive an ancient art form. Their work, however, ended up launching a whole new genre that would eventually spread across Europe and become hugely popular. So in a way, opera is a classic case of an experiment that had unintended consequences.

title: The Influence of German Expressionism on Film Noir
passage:
Okay, so today we're going to look at how German Expressionism, a movement that flourished in the 1920s, left a lasting mark on American film noir. Now, you might be wondering, what exactly is German Expressionism? Well, it's a style that emerged in Germany after World War I, characterized by distorted sets, high-contrast lighting, and a focus on psychological themes like madness and paranoia. Think of films like 'The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari' – the crooked streets, the shadows painted on walls – all meant to reflect inner turmoil. 

Now, how did this influence film noir? Many German directors, like Fritz Lang and F.W. Murnau, emigrated to Hollywood in the 1920s and 30s, fleeing political unrest. They brought their visual style with them. Film noir, which peaked in the 1940s and 50s, adopted those same techniques: chiaroscuro lighting, where light and dark are starkly contrasted; unusual camera angles; and a sense of moral ambiguity. But there's a key difference. In German Expressionism, the distortion was often fantastical, set in imaginary worlds. In film noir, these techniques were applied to realistic, contemporary American settings – city streets, detective offices – to show corruption and alienation. So, while the style was imported, its purpose shifted. It's a great example of how cinematic movements cross borders and evolve.

title: The Secret Life of the Naked Mole Rat
passage: Professor: Today we're going to look at a creature that breaks almost every rule we associate with mammals. The naked mole rat. It's a small, hairless rodent found in East Africa, and it lives in underground colonies that can number up to three hundred individuals. Now, what's remarkable is that only one female, the queen, reproduces. All the others—males and females—are workers. They dig tunnels, gather food, and care for the young. This is called eusociality, and it's common in insects like ants and bees, but extremely rare in mammals. Another oddity: naked mole rats are cold-blooded, sort of. They can't regulate their body temperature like we do. So they huddle together to stay warm, or bask in shallow tunnels to cool down. And they hardly ever get cancer. Researchers have found that their cells produce a special sugar that stops tumors from forming. So you can see why scientists are so interested in these animals.

title: The Hidden Language of Plant Defense: Talking Trees
passage: Okay, let's pick up where we left off last time. I want to talk about something that sounds like science fiction but is actually well-documented in plant biology: plant communication. Specifically, how trees warn each other about insect attacks. Now, you might think plants are passive, just sitting there. But take the acacia tree in the African savanna. When a giraffe starts nibbling on its leaves, the acacia releases a chemical called ethylene into the air. This isn't just a random gas—it's a distress signal. Nearby acacias detect this ethylene and immediately start pumping tannins into their leaves. Tannins are bitter and toxic to many herbivores, so the giraffe moves on. But here's the kicker: the giraffe doesn't just move to the next tree downwind. It actually walks upwind, against the wind, to find trees that haven't received the warning yet. That's a learned behavior, not instinct—giraffes have figured out the communication system. This suggests a kind of evolutionary arms race. The trees evolve chemical signals, and the herbivores evolve counter-strategies. So next time you're in a forest, remember: it's not silent. It's a noisy conversation we just can't hear.

title: Feathered Dinosaurs and the Origin of Flight
passage: Okay, so today we're going to talk about a discovery that really shook up the world of paleontology back in the 1990s. For a long time, we thought dinosaurs were just giant, scaly reptiles. But then, in China, paleontologists started unearthing fossils with clear impressions of feathers. Not just a few filaments, but fully modern-looking feathers with a central shaft and barbs. Now, these weren't from birds—they were from small, meat-eating dinosaurs. So the question became: why would a non-flying dinosaur have feathers? The traditional answer was insulation—keeping warm. That makes sense for small, active animals. But here's the twist: some of these dinosaurs, like Microraptor, had feathers on all four limbs—wings on both arms and legs. And the feathers were asymmetrical, which is a hallmark of flight feathers in modern birds. So some paleontologists proposed that these dinosaurs could glide from tree to tree. Others argued they ran along the ground and used their wings to help them leap. This is the famous 'trees-down' versus 'ground-up' debate. But what's really interesting is that recent studies of the feather structure suggest they might have first evolved for display—like a peacock's tail—to attract mates or scare rivals. So feathers may have started as a visual signal, and only later were co-opted for flight. That's a pretty big shift from the old idea that flight was the primary driver.

title: The Science of Atmospheric Rivers
passage: Professor: Today we're going to talk about a weather phenomenon that you might not have heard of, but it has a huge impact on the West Coast of the United States: atmospheric rivers. An atmospheric river is basically a long, narrow corridor of concentrated water vapor in the atmosphere. These rivers in the sky can transport as much water as the Amazon River discharges into the ocean. When they make landfall, they can produce heavy rain and snow, sometimes causing floods. But they're not all bad. In fact, they provide a significant portion of California's annual water supply. Without them, the state would face severe droughts. So why are they called rivers? Because they are relatively narrow, about 300 to 500 kilometers wide, and they stretch for thousands of kilometers. They form over the ocean, often in the tropics, and are carried by prevailing winds toward the poles. One famous atmospheric river event in 1861-62 caused massive flooding in California, turning the Central Valley into a lake. So as you can see, these are powerful and important weather systems.

title: The Bioluminescent Bay: A Fragile Ecosystem
passage: Okay, so today we're going to talk about bioluminescent bays, specifically the famous one in Puerto Rico called Mosquito Bay. Now, bioluminescence is the production of light by living organisms. In this bay, the light is produced by a type of dinoflagellate, a microscopic plankton called Pyrodinium bahamense. When these organisms are disturbed—say, by a kayak paddle or a swimming fish—they emit a blue-green light. It's a chemical reaction involving a molecule called luciferin and an enzyme called luciferase. But here's the thing: this bay is extremely fragile. The dinoflagellates need specific conditions: a narrow inlet, mangrove forests that provide nutrients, and very little water movement. Any change—like pollution, boat traffic, or even too many tourists swimming—can disrupt the environment. In fact, in 2016, the bay went completely dark for a while, likely due to a combination of drought and human activity. So, while the glowing water is a spectacular sight, it's also a warning sign. These ecosystems are rare and easily damaged. And that's why conservation efforts are so critical. Now, before we go further, any questions?

title: The Physics of Sonic Booms
passage:
Today we're going to talk about sonic booms, a phenomenon that occurs when an object travels through the air faster than the speed of sound. Now, you might think that a sonic boom is created only at the moment an aircraft breaks the sound barrier, but that's a common misconception. Actually, a sonic boom is continuous as long as the aircraft remains supersonic. 

Let me explain. When an object moves through air, it creates pressure waves that travel outward in all directions at the speed of sound. If the object is slower than sound, these waves spread out ahead of it. But when the object reaches the speed of sound, the waves can't get out of the way fast enough. They compress into a single shock wave, a cone-shaped wave front that trails behind the aircraft. This shock wave is what we hear as a sonic boom. 

So why is it continuous? Because the aircraft is constantly producing new pressure waves as it moves. As long as it stays supersonic, it keeps generating that shock wave, and an observer on the ground will hear a boom when the cone passes over them. In fact, the boom is heard along the entire flight path, not just at the moment of breaking the sound barrier. 

This has practical implications. For example, supersonic flights over land are often restricted because the continuous boom can be disruptive. That's why Concorde, the famous supersonic passenger jet, was only allowed to fly supersonic over the ocean.

title: The Role of Micrometeorites in Earth's Geological History
passage: Professor: Today, we're going to talk about something that might seem insignificant but actually plays a crucial role in Earth's geological history: micrometeorites. These are tiny particles, typically less than a millimeter in size, that survive their passage through the atmosphere and land on Earth's surface. Now, you might be wondering, how much material are we talking about? Well, it's estimated that about 3,000 to 7,000 tons of micrometeorites reach Earth's surface every year. That's a lot! But here's the thing: most people think of meteorites as large, dramatic rocks, but micrometeorites are far more abundant. They're basically cosmic dust. And because they're so small, they cool down quickly and don't burn up entirely, so they preserve their original composition. This makes them valuable for studying the early solar system. For example, some micrometeorites contain organic compounds, which could have contributed to the origin of life on Earth. Also, they can be found in deep-sea sediments and polar ice, providing a record of past cosmic activity. So, next time you see a shooting star, remember that a tiny piece of it might just land near you.

title: The Sociology of Competitive Eating Contests
passage: Professor: Today we're diving into a rather unusual topic—competitive eating contests. Now, before you dismiss this as mere entertainment, sociologists study these events to understand broader social dynamics. For instance, consider the annual Nathan's Hot Dog Eating Contest. It's not just about how many hot dogs someone can eat in ten minutes. It's a microcosm of American culture: individualism, spectacle, and the celebration of excess. But here's a twist: in Japan, competitive eating is often framed as a display of discipline and technique. Competitors train rigorously, and the emphasis is on precision—how efficiently they can consume, not just how much. So the same activity takes on different meanings across cultures. Another aspect is the audience. In the U.S., the crowd cheers for the underdog and revels in the messiness. In Japan, audiences appreciate the athletes' focus and calm demeanor. This reflects deeper cultural values: American individualism versus Japanese collectivism. Moreover, sponsorship and media play a huge role. In the U.S., events are heavily commercialized, with corporate logos everywhere. In Japan, they're often televised as serious sports, with less overt branding. So next time you watch a hot dog eating contest, think about what it says about the society that produces it.

title: The History of the Silk Road: More Than Just Silk
passage: Professor: Today we're going to talk about the Silk Road. Now, when most people hear that term, they immediately think of silk—this luxurious fabric that was traded from China to the West. And yes, silk was a major commodity. But the Silk Road was about much more than just silk. In fact, it was a vast network of trade routes that connected East Asia, India, Persia, Arabia, and Europe for over a thousand years. And what's really fascinating is that it wasn't just goods that moved along these routes. Ideas, technologies, religions, and even diseases traveled too. For example, papermaking technology spread from China to the Islamic world and eventually to Europe. Buddhism traveled from India to China along these same routes. And unfortunately, the plague—the Black Death—also made its way from Asia to Europe in the 14th century. So the Silk Road was essentially the internet of its time, facilitating exchange on a massive scale. Now, one common misconception is that the Silk Road was a single, well-defined road. In reality, it was a shifting network of paths that changed depending on political conditions, geography, and climate. Merchants rarely traveled the entire route; instead, goods were passed along from one trading hub to another, like a relay race. So when we study the Silk Road, we're really studying a complex system of cultural and economic exchange, not just a simple trade route.

title: Office Hours: Research Paper Topic Discussion
passage:
Student: Professor, do you have a minute? I'm having trouble narrowing down my research paper topic for your environmental policy class.
Professor: Sure, come in. What are you thinking about?
Student: Well, I'm interested in renewable energy, but that's too broad. I need something more specific.
Professor: Right. What aspect of renewable energy? Policy, technology, economics?
Student: Probably policy. I read about Germany's feed-in tariff system, but I'm not sure if that's too narrow.
Professor: Actually, that could work. But you'd need to focus on a specific outcome. For example, how the policy affected solar adoption in a particular region.
Student: That makes sense. I could compare two regions in Germany. But is it okay to use a single country as a case study?
Professor: Absolutely, as long as you draw broader lessons. You might also look at whether the policy led to unintended consequences, like higher electricity prices.
Student: Good point. I'll start with a literature review to see what's been written.
Professor: Perfect. And remember, the paper is due in four weeks, so don't spend too long on the review. Set a deadline for yourself.
Student: Thanks, Professor. I'll email you a draft outline next week.

title: Library Help for a Research Paper
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a librarian.

Student: Hi, I'm working on a paper for my Environmental Science class about urban air quality. I need to find some peer-reviewed articles, but I'm not sure where to start.

Librarian: Sure, I can help. Have you used our library databases before?

Student: A little, but I usually just search Google Scholar. My professor said we need at least five scholarly sources, and they have to be recent—within the last five years.

Librarian: Okay. For environmental science, I'd recommend starting with Environmental Sciences Database and JSTOR. You can filter by publication date and peer-reviewed. Also, check the subject terms—sometimes 'air pollution' and 'urban air quality' bring up different results.

Student: Good to know. What about books? Are they considered scholarly?

Librarian: They can be, but for a short paper, journal articles are usually more efficient. If you do use books, look for academic publishers, like university presses.

Student: Got it. One more thing—can I access these databases from home?

Librarian: Yes, with your student ID and password. If you have trouble, you can chat with a librarian online. We're available 24/7.

Student: That's great. Thanks so much!

Librarian: You're welcome. Good luck with your paper.

title: Dorm Room Change Request

title: Writing Center Session: Revising a Paper
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a writing center tutor.

Student: Hi, I have an appointment. I'm working on a paper for my sociology class, and I'm really stuck.

Tutor: Sure, have a seat. What's the paper about?

Student: It's about the effects of remote work on urban economies. I have a lot of data, but my professor said my argument isn't clear. I don't know how to fix it.

Tutor: Okay, let's look at your thesis. Can you read it to me?

Student: "Remote work has changed cities." That's it.

Tutor: Hmm. That's a bit broad. A strong thesis should take a specific position. What exactly do you want to argue?

Student: Well, I think remote work is actually helping smaller cities because people are moving there. But it's hurting downtown businesses in big cities.

Tutor: That's a great argument. You should put that in your thesis. So something like, "While remote work benefits smaller cities by attracting new residents, it harms large-city downtowns by reducing foot traffic."

Student: That sounds much better. But then my body paragraphs—do I need to change them?

Tutor: Not necessarily. You just need to make sure each paragraph connects back to that main argument. Right now, your second paragraph is all about tax policies. How does that relate?

Student: I guess it shows how smaller cities can use tax breaks to attract remote workers.

Tutor: Exactly. So make that link explicit. Also, your conclusion just repeats the introduction. Try to end with a recommendation or a prediction.

Student: Okay, I think I know what to do now. Thank you!

title: Transferring Credits at a New University
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and an admissions advisor.

Student: Hi, I'm transferring from another university, and I'm a bit confused about how my credits will transfer. Could you help me?

Advisor: Of course. We generally accept credits from accredited institutions if the courses are comparable to ours. Can you tell me which courses you're concerned about?

Student: Well, I took a course called 'Introduction to Environmental Science' that had a lab component. It was four credits. Will that count toward my major here?

Advisor: Let me check. Our equivalent course is 'Environmental Science 101' with a lab, also four credits. That should transfer directly. But I need to see the syllabus to confirm the lab hours match. 

Student: Okay, I can email that. What about my English composition course? I took it online, and I heard online courses might not transfer.

Advisor: That depends. If the course was from an accredited school and the learning outcomes are the same, it can transfer. We just need the official transcript and a course description. But some departments have restrictions on online labs, not typically on composition.

Student: Got it. So I should gather all my syllabi and transcripts?

Advisor: Exactly. Submit them to the registrar's office. They'll do an initial evaluation, and then you can appeal if any credits are denied. The process takes about two weeks.

Student: Thanks. That's really helpful.

title: Alumni Career Planning Conversation
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and an alumnus.

Student: Excuse me, Mr. Harrison? I'm Emily, a junior majoring in environmental science. I saw your talk on campus about sustainability consulting. Could I ask you a few questions about your career path?

Alumnus: Of course, Emily. I graduated with the same major ten years ago. What's on your mind?

Student: I'm torn between going to grad school right away and getting some work experience first. What did you do?

Alumnus: I worked for two years at a nonprofit focused on water conservation. Honestly, that experience taught me more about project management and community engagement than any classroom could. But I did go back for a master's later, and that helped me specialize in corporate sustainability.

Student: So you'd recommend working first?

Alumnus: Not necessarily. It depends on your goals. If you want to do research or teach, going straight to grad school makes sense. But for consulting, practical experience is key. Also, many firms now offer tuition reimbursement for part-time master's programs.

Student: That's good to know. What skills should I build now?

Alumnus: Data analysis is huge. And learn to communicate with non-experts. I use both every day. Also, don't underestimate networking—that's how I got my current job.

title: TA Meeting About Research Paper
passage: Hey, thanks for coming in. So, I looked over your draft, and overall, it's a solid start. You've got a clear thesis, and your sources are relevant. But I think the main issue is that you're trying to cover too much. You've got three case studies, and each one could be its own paper. For a 10-page assignment, that's just not realistic. I'd suggest picking one case study and going deeper — maybe the one on urban farming in Detroit. That seems to have the most data. Also, your literature review is a bit thin. You cite five sources, but for a paper like this, you should aim for at least ten. And make sure they're from peer-reviewed journals, not just news articles. I noticed a couple of those. One more thing: your conclusion just restates the intro. Try to offer some practical implications or future research directions. That'll make it stronger. Does that make sense?

title: Planning a Class Presentation
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and his professor.

Student: Professor Lee, do you have a minute? I'm working on my presentation for next week's environmental science class, and I'm a bit stuck on the structure.

Professor: Of course, come in. What's the topic again?

Student: I'm arguing that urban green roofs can significantly reduce city temperatures. I've got lots of data, but I'm not sure how to present it without overwhelming everyone.

Professor: That's a common problem. Remember, a presentation isn't a data dump. Start with a clear hook—maybe a striking statistic about heat waves. Then, give just two or three key examples, like Chicago's City Hall or Singapore's rooftop gardens. Visuals help, but keep them simple.

Student: Should I include the counterarguments? Like the high installation costs?

Professor: Absolutely. Acknowledging limitations makes your argument stronger. But don't spend too long on them—maybe one slide. End with a call to action or a question for the audience.

Student: That makes sense. I was worried about timing too. I have ten minutes.

Professor: Then practice with a timer. Cut any details that don't directly support your main point. And remember, you're not just informing—you're persuading. So your enthusiasm matters as much as your facts.

Student: Thanks, Professor. I feel much better now.

choices.label: B

choices.label: D

title: Library Research for a Paper

Student: Okay. One more thing—I need to cite my sources in APA format. Do you have a guide?

title: Discussing Financial Aid Options
passage:
Student: Hi, I'm here about the financial aid package. I got an email saying I need to submit some additional documents, but I'm not sure what exactly is missing.

Advisor: Sure, let me pull up your file. Okay, I see you've submitted the FAFSA and the institutional aid form. The issue is that we still need your parents' most recent tax return. Without it, we can't verify your Expected Family Contribution.

Advisor: That would work, but it needs to be the signed copy. Also, you should know that if you're applying for the work-study program, there's a separate deadline this Friday. The general aid application deadline is next Wednesday, so you have a bit more time for that.

Student: Got it. And what about the scholarship application? I heard there's a merit-based one for continuing students.

Advisor: Yes, the Continuing Student Scholarship. That requires a separate essay and a recommendation letter. But the deadline for that isn't until the end of the month, so you can focus on the tax return first. Once you submit it, we can finalize your aid package.

Student: Thanks, I'll bring the tax return tomorrow and start on the scholarship essay this weekend. I appreciate your help.

title: Career Fair Follow-Up
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a career advisor.

Advisor: Hi, come on in. What can I do for you?

Student: Hi, I’m a junior in environmental science. I went to the career fair last week and talked to a few companies, but I’m not sure what to do next. One recruiter from GreenGrid Energy said they have summer internships, but she told me to apply online. Should I just submit my resume and wait?

Advisor: Not exactly. Did you get her business card?

Student: Yeah, I did. It’s right here.

Advisor: Good. The online application is only the first step. You should email her directly within 48 hours, remind her where you met, and attach your resume. Mention one specific thing you discussed—maybe the smart meter project she described. That shows you were paying attention.

Student: Okay, I can do that. But my resume is pretty general. I don’t have much experience.

Advisor: That’s fine for an internship. Focus on your coursework and any group projects. Did you do that campus energy audit last semester?

Student: Yes, I helped collect data on lighting usage in dorms.

Advisor: Perfect. That’s directly relevant. Put it under a “Projects” section, and quantify the results if you can. Also, tailor your resume for each company. Don’t send the same version everywhere.

Student: I see. And should I follow up again if she doesn’t reply?

Advisor: Yes, after one week. But keep it short and polite. If you still hear nothing, move on. There are other internships—I can send you a list.

Student: That would be great. Thanks!

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the conversation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To complain about the career fair organization.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To get advice on following up after meeting a recruiter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To apply for a job at the career services office.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To discuss changing her major to environmental science.

title: Choosing a Major: A Conversation with an Academic Advisor
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and an academic advisor.

Student: Hi, Professor Martinez. Do you have a minute?

Advisor: Of course, come in. What's on your mind?

Student: I'm having trouble deciding on a major. I'm interested in both biology and environmental science, but I can't choose.

Advisor: That's a common dilemma. Have you looked at the requirements for each?

Student: Yes, and they overlap a lot. But I'm worried about career prospects. Biology seems more versatile.

Advisor: Actually, environmental science is growing fast, especially with the focus on climate change. But have you considered a double major? You already have credits in both.

Student: I thought about it, but I'm afraid it's too much work. I also want to study abroad next year.

Advisor: Study abroad can count toward either major if you choose the right courses. For example, a tropical ecology program in Costa Rica would fit both. As for the workload, you could take some summer classes to lighten the load.

Student: That's a great idea. I didn't know summer classes could help. But will it delay my graduation?

Advisor: Not if you plan carefully. Let's map out a four-year plan together. First, let's list the required courses for both majors and see where they overlap. Then we can decide if a double major is feasible.

Student: Okay, that sounds doable. Thanks for your help.

Advisor: My pleasure. Let's meet again next week with a draft plan.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is failing his biology class.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: He needs help finding a summer internship.

title: Writing Center Consultation
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a writing center tutor.

Student: Hi, I'm here about my history paper. I got the draft back with a lot of comments, and I'm not sure where to start.

Tutor: Sure, let's take a look. What was the assignment?

Student: We had to analyze the causes of the Industrial Revolution. I wrote about technological innovations, but the professor said my thesis was too broad. I argued that inventions like the steam engine caused it, but she said I need to narrow it down.

Tutor: I see. So you're saying the steam engine was a cause, but you're not specifying which aspect? Like, did it affect transportation, manufacturing, or something else?

Student: Exactly. I just said 'technological innovations' without focusing.

Tutor: Okay, so for revision, you could pick one specific innovation, like the power loom in textile production, and show how it directly led to factory system changes. That would make your argument more precise.

Student: That makes sense. But I also have trouble with my conclusion. I just restated my thesis.

Tutor: A conclusion should do more than repeat. You could discuss broader implications, like how the factory system influenced urbanisation or labor conditions. That would add depth.

Student: Got it. So I need to narrow my thesis and expand my conclusion. Thanks!

questions.question: What is the main problem with the student's paper?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The thesis is too broad.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The evidence is insufficient.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The conclusion is too long.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The writing style is informal.

questions.explanation: 考点：主旨题。对话开头学生说教授认为他的论点太宽泛（thesis was too broad），辅导老师也确认了这一点。B选项证据不足未提及；C选项结论太长与原文不符（学生说只是重复论点）；D选项写作风格不正式未提及。

questions.question: What specific advice does the tutor give about the thesis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Change the topic to a different revolution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Focus on one innovation, like the power loom.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Include more statistical data.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Compare multiple causes equally.

questions.explanation: 考点：细节题。辅导老师建议学生选择一个具体的创新，比如纺织生产中的动力织布机（power loom），并说明它如何直接导致工厂制度的变化。A选项改变主题未提及；C选项加入统计数据未提及；D选项平等比较多个原因与建议相反。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the student's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is missing from the draft.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It introduces a new argument.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It merely repeats the thesis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the strongest part of the paper.

questions.explanation: 考点：推断题。学生说他的结论只是重述了论点（I just restated my thesis），辅导老师也指出结论应该做更多，比如讨论更广泛的影响。因此可以推断结论仅仅是重复论点。A选项结论缺失与原文不符；B选项引入新论点未提及；D选项结论是最强部分与原文相反。

title: IT Help Desk: Laptop Repair
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and an IT technician at the university help desk.

Student: Hi, I'm here about my laptop. It's been really slow, and sometimes it just freezes. I have a paper due next week, and I can't afford to lose any work.

Technician: I see. Have you backed up your files recently?

Student: No, not really. I've just been saving everything on the desktop.

Technician: That's risky. First, let's back up your important files to an external drive. Then I'll run a diagnostic. It sounds like you might have a virus or too many startup programs.

Student: Oh, I did download some free software last month. Could that be the problem?

Technician: Possibly. We'll check that. Also, how old is your laptop?

Student: About four years. I've never had it serviced.

Technician: That could be part of it. Dust buildup can cause overheating and slowdowns. I'll clean the fan and check the hard drive. If it's failing, we might need to replace it.

Student: How long will that take?

Technician: If it's just a cleanup, about an hour. If we need to replace the hard drive, it could take a day or two. But we'll keep your data safe.

Student: Okay, I really need it for my paper. Can you prioritize it?

Technician: Sure, I'll put a rush on it. Just fill out this form, and I'll get started right away.

title: Transferring Credits
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a university transfer advisor.

Student: Hi, I'm hoping you can help me. I just transferred here from a community college, and I'm trying to figure out which of my credits will actually count toward my degree.

Advisor: Sure, I can help with that. Do you have your official transcript with you?

Student: Yes, here it is. I took a lot of general education courses, like English Composition, College Algebra, and Introduction to Psychology.

Advisor: Okay, let me take a look. Hmm, English Comp and Psych should transfer directly. But College Algebra... it looks like you took a version that's considered developmental, so it might not count toward your major requirements.

Student: Oh no, that's a problem. I need that for my business degree. Is there any way to appeal?

Advisor: You can file a petition with the department. But honestly, it might be easier to just retake a higher-level math course here. That would satisfy the requirement and boost your GPA.

Student: I see. What about my history course? I took Western Civilization.

Advisor: That one transfers as a humanities elective, not as a history major requirement. But since you're not a history major, it should still count as a general elective.

Student: Got it. So I should focus on the math issue first?

Advisor: Exactly. And make sure to submit your petition before the end of the second week of classes. Otherwise, you'll have to wait until next semester.

title: Alumni Career Advising Session
passage:

Student: Hi, I'm here for the career advising session. I'm a junior in computer science, and I'm not sure what to do after graduation.

title: Graduation Requirement Inquiry
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and an academic advisor.

Student: Hi, Professor Davis. I'm here to talk about my graduation requirements. I'm a senior, and I'm a bit worried I might not have everything I need to graduate this spring.

Advisor: Of course, come in. Let's take a look at your transcript. What's your major?

Student: Environmental Science. I've completed all the core courses and most of the electives, but I'm not sure about the foreign language requirement. I took Spanish for two years in high school, but I didn't continue here.

Advisor: Ah, that's a common issue. The university requires two semesters of a foreign language at the college level, unless you pass a placement exam. High school courses don't automatically count.

Student: Oh no. So I need to take two more Spanish classes? But I'm graduating in May. That's only one semester left.

Advisor: Actually, you can take a placement exam. If you test into the second semester, you only need to take one course. And you could take it this summer and still walk in May, but you'd receive your diploma after the summer session.

Student: Hmm, walking in May is important to my family. So if I take the exam and pass, I can enroll in one Spanish course this summer?

Advisor: Exactly. But you also need to fulfill the writing intensive requirement. I see you've taken two writing courses, but you need three. You could take a third one online this summer as well.

Student: Okay, so two courses this summer. That's doable. Thanks for clarifying. I feel much better now.

Advisor: No problem. Make sure to register for the placement exam soon. The deadline is next Friday.

title: International Student Visa Problem
passage:
Listen to a conversation between a student and an international student advisor.

Student: Hi, I'm here because I'm worried about my visa status. I just realized my I-20 form expires next month, but I still have one more semester to finish.

Advisor: Oh, that's a common issue. You need to apply for an extension before your current I-20 expires. Have you talked to the international office about this?

Student: No, I haven't. I thought I just needed to renew my visa stamp, but my friend said that's different.

Advisor: Right. The visa stamp in your passport is for entry, but your I-20 is what keeps you in legal status while you're here. If it expires, you could fall out of status, which is serious.

Student: So what should I do?

Advisor: First, get a new I-20 from the international office. You'll need to show proof of funding for the next semester. Then, if your visa stamp is also expired, you'll need to renew it if you travel outside the U.S. But you can stay here as long as your I-20 is valid.

Student: Okay, so I should go to the international office first?

Advisor: Exactly. And do it soon. Don't wait until the last minute. Also, make sure you don't work off-campus without authorization, as that can also affect your status.

Student: Thanks. I'll go there tomorrow.

choices.text: The student's I-20 form is about to expire.

title: Choosing a Topic for a Class Presentation
passage:
Professor: Hi, Jamie. Come in. You wanted to talk about your presentation for next month?
Student: Yes, Professor. I'm having trouble deciding on a topic. The assignment says to analyze a social issue, but I don't know which one to pick.
Professor: Well, what are you interested in? Something you already know a bit about might be easier to research.
Student: I've been reading a lot about food waste lately. Like how much food supermarkets throw away.
Professor: That's a great topic—very relevant. But you'll need to narrow it down. Are you focusing on supermarkets, restaurants, or households?
Student: I was thinking supermarkets. But is that too narrow? I mean, will I find enough sources?
Professor: Actually, there's plenty of research on retail food waste. You could look at causes and possible solutions. Just make sure you don't just describe the problem—you need to analyze it.
Student: Got it. So I should argue something, like whether tax incentives would help reduce waste?
Professor: Exactly. And remember, the presentation is only ten minutes, so keep it focused. Also, I recommend you submit your outline by next Friday for feedback.
Student: I'll do that. Thanks, Professor.

title: Requesting a Dormitory Room Change

title: Office Hours: Research Paper Discussion
passage:
Professor: Hi, come in. You wanted to talk about your research paper?
Student: Yes, Professor. I'm a bit confused about the methodology section. I'm planning to survey students about their sleep habits, but I'm not sure how many participants I need.
Professor: That's a common concern. It depends on your research question. Are you looking at correlations or just descriptive statistics?
Student: I want to see if there's a relationship between sleep duration and GPA.
Professor: Then you'll need a sample size that gives you enough statistical power. Generally, for a correlation study, you'd want at least 100 participants. But remember, it's not just about the number—it's also about how you select them. Random sampling is ideal.
Student: I see. Also, should I use an online questionnaire or paper-based?
Professor: Online is more efficient and you can reach more people. But be mindful of response bias. Maybe include some open-ended questions to get richer data.
Student: That makes sense. One more thing: how should I structure the literature review?
Professor: Organize it thematically, not chronologically. Group studies by key themes, and show how they connect to your research gap. That will make your argument stronger.
Student: Great, thank you. I'll revise my draft accordingly.
Professor: You're welcome. Feel free to email me if you have more questions.

title: Writing Center Consultation on a Research Paper
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a writing center tutor.

Student: Hi, I'm here about my research paper for Professor Miller's sociology class. I'm really struggling with the organization, and I have a draft due next week.

Tutor: Sure, I can help. Do you have your draft with you?

Student: Yes, here it is. I feel like my argument is all over the place. I have a lot of information, but I'm not sure how to connect it.

Tutor: Okay, let me take a quick look. Hmm, I see. Your thesis is about the impact of social media on political polarization, right?

Student: Exactly. I argue that echo chambers on platforms like Twitter and Facebook have intensified division. But my paragraphs jump from statistics to anecdotes without clear transitions.

Tutor: That's a common issue. One thing you could do is create an outline that maps each paragraph to a specific sub-claim. For example, start with a paragraph defining echo chambers, then present evidence for increased polarization, and finally address counterarguments.

Student: That makes sense. I also worry about my conclusion. It just repeats the introduction. How can I make it more effective?

Tutor: A strong conclusion should synthesize your main points and suggest implications or future research. Don't just restate—offer a new insight. For instance, you could discuss how platforms might redesign algorithms to reduce polarization.

Student: Great, I'll try that. Thanks so much!

Tutor: No problem. Feel free to come back with a revised draft.

title: A Campus Bookstore Conversation About Textbook Options
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a bookstore employee.

Student: Hi, I'm looking for the textbook for Introduction to Environmental Science. The course code is ENV 101.

Student: That's a big price difference. Does the 4th edition have the same content?

Employee: Most of the chapters are the same, but the 5th edition has an extra chapter on climate policy and updated case studies. Your professor might assign readings from that new chapter.

Student: Hmm, I see. Do you know if Professor Martinez requires the 5th edition?

Employee: I'm not sure. But I can tell you that last semester, many students bought the 4th edition and did fine. However, if you want to be safe, you could buy the 5th edition used and sell it back at the end of the semester. We buy back books for about 50% of the new price if they're in good condition.

Student: That's helpful. Actually, I think I'll check with the professor first before deciding. Thanks for the information.

Employee: You're welcome. Just so you know, the 4th edition copies are going fast. We only have a few left.

Student: Okay, I'll keep that in mind. Thanks again.

title: Preparing for a Class Presentation
passage:
Professor: Hi, come in. You wanted to talk about the presentation for next week?
Student: Yes, Professor. I'm doing my topic on urban beekeeping, but I'm not sure how to make it interesting. Last time I just read my notes and everyone looked bored.
Professor: Well, first, don't read from notes. Use slides with just a few keywords and images. And start with a surprising fact—like how many bee species live in cities.
Student: That's a good idea. But I only have ten minutes. Is it okay to use a video clip?
Professor: A short one, yes. Thirty seconds maximum. But make sure it supports your point, not just entertains.
Student: Got it. Also, should I include my own research from the community garden?
Professor: Absolutely. That's what makes your talk unique. But don't just list data. Tell a story—like how you first got stung and then learned to work with the bees.
Student: That sounds better. I was worried about the Q&A part. What if I don't know the answer?
Professor: Just say you'll look it up. That's fine. And practice your timing. Come to my office hours on Friday and we can run through it once.
Student: Thank you. I'll do that.

title: Finding Sources for a Paper on Urban Beekeeping
passage: Librarian: Hi, how can I help you today? Student: Hi, I'm working on a paper about urban beekeeping, and I'm having trouble finding sources. My professor said I need at least five peer-reviewed articles, but I'm only finding news articles and blog posts. Librarian: Okay, let's see what we can do. Are you searching the general database or a specific one? Student: I tried the main search box on the library homepage. Librarian: That searches everything, which can be overwhelming. For peer-reviewed articles, you should use specialized databases like Environmental Sciences or Academic Search Complete. Also, try keywords like 'urban apiculture' instead of 'urban beekeeping'—that's the scientific term. Student: Oh, I didn't know that. And how do I filter for peer-reviewed? Librarian: In most databases, there's a checkbox for 'peer-reviewed' or 'scholarly journals' on the left side. Also, you can limit the publication date to the last ten years to keep it current. Student: Great. What about books? My professor mentioned some books might be useful. Librarian: Yes, we have a few. But remember, books can take longer to publish, so they might not have the latest research. For a paper like yours, I'd focus on articles first. Student: That makes sense. One more thing: I need to cite in APA style. Do you have a guide? Librarian: Absolutely. We have an online APA guide, and you can also sign up for a citation workshop next week. Student: Perfect. Thanks so much! Librarian: You're welcome. Good luck with your paper!

title: Dormitory Room Change Request
passage:

title: Joining the Debate Society

title: Choosing a Major: Academic Advising Session

title: Exchange Program Advising Session
passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Martinez. Thanks for seeing me during office hours. I wanted to ask about the exchange program with the University of Barcelona. I'm a junior majoring in international relations, and I've been thinking about applying for next spring.

Professor: Of course, happy to help. Have you looked at the requirements yet? The program is competitive, and there are a few specific things you need to prepare.

Student: I did read through the brochure, but I'm a bit confused about the language requirement. My Spanish is only at the intermediate level. Is that enough?

Professor: That's actually the minimum. You need at least two semesters of intermediate Spanish, or equivalent proficiency. But I should mention that most courses at Barcelona are taught in Spanish, so stronger fluency will make your life much easier.

Student: I see. And what about the application deadline?

Professor: For spring semester, all materials must be submitted by October 15th. That includes a statement of purpose, two recommendation letters, and your transcript. The good news is that your GPA of 3.6 is well above the minimum of 3.0.

Student: Great. One more thing—can I take courses related to my major there, or only language classes?

Professor: You can take major-related courses, but you need to get them pre-approved by the department. Otherwise, the credits might not transfer back. I strongly suggest you meet with your academic advisor before you leave.

Student: That's really helpful. I'll start working on my statement of purpose this week.

Professor: Good. And don't forget to ask your recommenders early—they're usually busy at the end of the semester.

title: Writing Center Session on Revising a Paper
passage:
W: Thanks for coming in. So, what are we working on today?
M: I have a history paper due next week, and I'm really struggling with the organization. The professor said my ideas are good, but they're all over the place.
W: Okay, let's take a look. Can you tell me what your main argument is?
M: Well, I'm arguing that the Industrial Revolution had a bigger impact on family structures than most historians admit. But I have so much evidence that I don't know how to fit it all in.
W: That's a common problem. You don't need to include everything. You should focus on the strongest three or four pieces of evidence.
M: But what about the counterarguments? My professor mentioned that a good paper should address opposing views.
W: Absolutely. You can put those in a separate paragraph near the end. But don't let them overshadow your own argument. Also, your introduction needs a clearer thesis statement. Right now, it's buried in the third paragraph.
M: So I should move it to the beginning?
W: Yes, and make it more specific. Instead of saying 'family structures changed,' say exactly how they changed, like 'the shift from extended families to nuclear families.'
M: That makes sense. I'll revise the introduction and reorganize the body paragraphs.
W: Good. And remember, I'm available for another session next Tuesday if you want feedback on the revised draft.
M: I'll definitely sign up. Thanks!

title: Requesting a Medical Leave of Absence
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a university advisor.

Student: Hi, Professor Martinez. Do you have a minute? I need to talk about something important.

Advisor: Of course, come in. What's going on?

Student: Well, I've been having some health issues lately, and my doctor recommended I take a leave of absence for the rest of the semester. I wanted to ask if it's possible to withdraw from my courses without failing them.

Advisor: I'm sorry to hear that. Yes, there is a medical withdrawal process. You'll need to submit a form signed by your doctor, and then the registrar will review it. If approved, you'll receive 'W' grades, which don't affect your GPA.

Student: That's a relief. But what about my scholarship? I'm worried I might lose it if I'm not enrolled full-time.

Advisor: Good question. You should contact the financial aid office directly. They have procedures for medical leaves that usually allow you to keep your scholarship, but you need to notify them as soon as possible.

Student: Okay, I'll do that today. And when can I return?

Advisor: You can re-enroll next semester if your doctor clears you. Just make sure to complete the readmission form by the deadline.

Student: Thank you so much. I feel much better now.

title: Credit Transfer Meeting
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a university admissions advisor.

Student: Hi, I'm transferring from another university, and I was told I need to meet with you about my credits. 

Advisor: That's right. I have your transcript here. So you've completed 45 credits at your previous school. Let's see... You took Introduction to Psychology, English Composition, and Calculus I. Those should transfer directly. 

Student: Great! What about my chemistry course? It was a different title—General Chemistry with Lab. 

Advisor: Hmm, our equivalent is Principles of Chemistry. The content looks similar, but I need to check if your lab hours match. Sometimes labs are shorter at other schools. 

Student: I think we had three hours of lab per week. 

Advisor: That should be fine, but I'll need to verify with the department. Also, your history course—World Civilizations—doesn't have a direct match here. We have a similar course, but it's a 200-level, and yours might be 100-level. So you might only get elective credit. 

Student: Oh, that's a bit disappointing. So I won't have to retake it? 

Advisor: No, you'll get credit, just not as a major requirement. You'll need to take one more history course if you want to fulfill the requirement. 

Student: I see. What about the credits that don't transfer? Do I lose them completely? 

Advisor: Not exactly. They can count as general electives, but there's a limit—only 12 elective credits can be applied. You have 15 that might fall into that category, so 3 credits might be lost. 

Student: Okay, that's good to know. Thanks for explaining everything.

passage:

Also, I noticed the second edition is still available. The content is about 90% the same. Some chapters are reordered, but the key concepts are identical.

Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a university parking office employee.

Student: Hi, I need to get a parking permit for this semester. I just moved off campus, and driving is the only way I can get to my morning classes now.

Employee: Sure. Are you a student? We have a few different options. The commuter permit is $120 for the semester, and it lets you park in the orange lots. The premium permit is $200, but it covers the garage next to the science building.

Student: I have classes mostly in the science building, but $200 is a lot. Is there any way to pay in installments?

Employee: Unfortunately, no. It has to be paid in full at the time you pick it up. But if you buy the commuter permit, you can still park in the garage after 4 p.m. and on weekends.

Student: That might work. My classes end at 3. Do I need to bring anything with me?

Employee: Yes. Your student ID and your vehicle registration. And make sure your account doesn't have any unpaid parking tickets.

Student: I think I have one from last month. I forgot to pay it.

Employee: Then you'll need to take care of that first. The system won't let me issue a permit if there's an outstanding balance.

Student: Okay, I'll pay it online tonight and come back tomorrow.

Employee: Perfect. We're open from 8 to 5.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the conversation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To ask about a parking ticket the student received.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To find out how to get a parking permit for the semester.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To complain about the cost of campus parking.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To apply for a job at the parking office.

questions.explanation: 主旨题。对话开头学生明确说“I need to get a parking permit for this semester”，随后整段对话都围绕如何办理停车证、费用、所需材料展开。A项停车罚单只是办理过程中的一个障碍，不是主旨；C项学生确实觉得贵，但没有抱怨，而是询问分期付款；D项完全无关。

questions.question: What is one advantage of the commuter permit mentioned by the employee?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It allows parking in the garage at all times.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It can be paid in monthly installments.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It permits garage parking after 4 p.m. and on weekends.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It includes a discount on future parking tickets.

questions.explanation: 细节题。员工在提到commuter permit时说“you can still park in the garage after 4 p.m. and on weekends”。A项“随时停”是premium permit才有的；B项员工明确说“no”分期付款；D项未提及罚单折扣。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the student?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The student will buy the premium permit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The student has already paid all parking tickets.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The student needs to resolve a payment issue before getting a permit.

choices.label: D

title: Meeting with a Teaching Assistant About a Late Assignment
passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Chen? I'm sorry to bother you. I know you're not the professor, but I saw your office said TA hours. I'm a bit confused about the lab report deadline. The syllabus says it's due Friday, but the online portal says Monday. Which one is correct? 
TA: Oh, hi. You're in the right place. I'm the TA for the course. Yeah, the professor extended the deadline to Monday because of the power outage last week. He sent an announcement. Did you not get it? 
Student: I must have missed that email. But that's a relief. I was worried I'd have to pull an all-nighter. So Monday by 11:59 PM? 
TA: Exactly. And remember, you need to submit both the PDF and the data file. Last semester, a lot of students only uploaded the PDF, and we had to deduct points. 
Student: Got it. I'll double-check. Also, is it okay if I use the data from the lab session I missed? I was sick that day. 
TA: You should use the data from the makeup lab you attended. If you didn't attend a makeup, you can't just use someone else's data. That would be academic dishonesty. Did you sign up for a makeup? 
Student: Yes, I did. I went last Wednesday. 
TA: Perfect. Then you're fine. Just make sure to cite the correct session date. 
Student: Thanks so much. I feel much better now.

questions.question: What is the main reason the student visits the teaching assistant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To ask for an extension on the lab report deadline

choices.label: B
choices.text: To clarify the correct due date for the lab report

choices.label: C
choices.text: To complain about the professor's announcement

choices.label: D
choices.text: To request permission to use another student's data

questions.explanation: 考点：主旨题。学生一开始就问“Which one is correct?”关于截止日期，因此主要目的是澄清正确的截止日期。A项：学生只是担心，但并未主动请求延期，截止日期已被教授延长。C项：学生没有抱怨，只是没看到通知。D项：学生询问是否可以使用自己缺课时的数据，但并非请求使用他人数据，且TA明确禁止，因此不是主要目的。

questions.question: According to the TA, what must students submit along with the PDF?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A printed copy of the lab report

choices.label: B
choices.text: A signed academic integrity form

choices.label: C
choices.text: The data file from the lab

choices.label: D
choices.text: A doctor's note for the missed lab

questions.explanation: 考点：细节题。TA明确说“you need to submit both the PDF and the data file”，因此C正确。A项未提及打印版。B项未提及诚信表格。D项未要求病假条，虽然学生提到生病，但TA只要求参加补做实验。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the student's lab data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The student will use data from the session they missed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The student will use data from a makeup lab session.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The student will borrow a friend's data with permission.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The student will redo the entire experiment alone.

questions.explanation: 考点：推断题。学生说“I went last Wednesday”参加补做实验，TA也确认“You should use the data from the makeup lab”，因此可推断学生将使用补做实验的数据。A项与事实相反，学生缺了课。C项被TA明确禁止。D项未提及重新独自做实验。

title: Course Registration Advising
passage:
Student: Hi, I'm a sophomore in computer science. I'm trying to register for next semester, but the system says I need an override for CS 201. I took the prerequisite, CS 101, last spring.

Advisor: Let me check. Ah, yes—CS 101 is listed as in progress on your record. The system doesn't accept it until grades are posted. Did you complete it?

Student: Yes, I finished it in May. But the grade might not have been uploaded yet because my professor was traveling.

Advisor: That happens. I can manually override the prerequisite if you show me your unofficial transcript. Do you have it with you?

Student: I have a PDF on my phone. Here.

Advisor: Great. I see an A. I'll approve the override. Also, CS 201 has two sections—one at 8 a.m. and one at 1 p.m. Which do you prefer?

Student: The 8 a.m. one fits my schedule better, but it's with Professor Lee. I've heard she's tough.

Advisor: She is challenging, but students say she's fair. The 1 p.m. section is with a new adjunct, so no reviews yet. Your choice.

Student: I'll take the 8 a.m. with Lee. I'd rather have a known quantity.

Advisor: Good. I'll process the override now. You should be able to register within an hour. Any other questions?

Student: No, that's all. Thanks!

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the student's visit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To complain about a professor's grading policy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To get help registering for a course that requires an override.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To change his major from computer science to another field.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To request a copy of his official transcript.

questions.explanation: 主旨题。学生开场即说明选课系统要求CS 201的override，需要教务处帮助解决，故选B。A未提及投诉评分；C未提转专业；D只是展示非正式成绩单，并非索要官方成绩单。

questions.question: Why does the system require an override for CS 201?

choices.text: The student did not take CS 101.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: CS 201 is restricted to juniors and seniors only.

questions.explanation: 细节题。顾问查看记录后指出CS 101显示为“in progress”，因为成绩尚未录入，所以系统不接受先修课完成。A与事实相反；B成绩是A，不低；D未提及年级限制。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the student's decision regarding the two sections of CS 201?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He chooses the 1 p.m. section because it has better reviews.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He chooses the 8 a.m. section because he prefers a professor with known feedback.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He decides not to take CS 201 this semester.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He chooses the 1 p.m. section because it fits his schedule better.

questions.explanation: 推断题。学生说8点的课更适合他的时间表，但听说Lee教授严格；然而1点的新兼职教师没有评价。他最终选择Lee教授，因为“宁愿选已知情况”，即偏好有已知反馈的教授。A错误，他选了8点；C错误，他决定选课；D错误，1点不是更适合，且他未选1点。

title: Consulting Internship Inquiry
passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Martinez. Do you have a moment? I wanted to ask about the consulting internship you mentioned in class last week.
Professor: Of course, come in. You're thinking of applying?
Student: Yes, but I'm a bit confused. The posting says it's for juniors and seniors, and I'm only a sophomore.
Professor: Ah, that's true for the formal program. But the company also has a separate summer analyst role specifically for sophomores. It's less structured, but it's a real project-based internship.
Student: Oh, I didn't see that. Where can I find it?
Professor: It's on their careers page under 'Early Insights.' The deadline is March 15th, so you still have two weeks.
Student: Great. Do you think my GPA is high enough? I have a 3.4.
Professor: The minimum is 3.2, so you're fine. But they really value analytical skills. Have you taken any statistics or data analysis courses?
Student: I'm taking Statistics 101 this semester, and I did a data project in my economics class.
Professor: Perfect. Highlight that project in your cover letter. Also, ask your economics professor for a recommendation—they prefer academic references.

Professor: Yes, it's a paid internship, and it can lead to a full-time offer after graduation.
Student: That sounds amazing. I'll start my application tonight.

title: Student Health Center Appointment
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a health center receptionist.

Receptionist: Good morning. Student Health Center. How can I help you?

Student: Hi, I'd like to schedule a physical exam. I'm applying for a summer internship and they require a health clearance form.

Receptionist: Sure. Are you a current student?

Student: Yes, I'm a junior. My student ID is 2-3-7-8-9-1.

Receptionist: Thanks. Let me check the doctor's availability. We have openings next Tuesday at 10 a.m. and Thursday at 2 p.m. Which works better?

Student: Thursday at 2 would be great. I have a lab until noon on Tuesday.

Receptionist: Okay, Thursday, the 15th, at 2 p.m. with Dr. Patel. The exam takes about 45 minutes. Please arrive 15 minutes early to fill out paperwork.

Student: Got it. Do I need to bring anything?

Receptionist: Yes, bring your insurance card and a photo ID. Also, avoid eating for at least two hours before the appointment because they'll check your blood sugar.

Student: No problem. And will the doctor sign the clearance form?

Receptionist: Yes, Dr. Patel can sign it after the exam, but you'll need to bring the form. We don't provide it.

title: Joining a Research Project in the Lab
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor.

Student: Professor Martinez, do you have a minute? I'm interested in joining your research project on plant genetics.

Professor: Oh, hi, Kevin. I remember you from last semester's biology class. You did well on the lab reports. But I have to tell you, the project is quite demanding. We meet three times a week, and you'll need to spend at least ten hours in the lab each week.

Student: That sounds fine. I've already completed most of my required courses, so I have time. Actually, I took a summer workshop on DNA extraction last year.

Professor: That's helpful. The project involves extracting DNA from local wildflowers and comparing their genetic diversity. But I should warn you, the first few weeks are mostly repetitive lab work—pipetting, centrifuging, that sort of thing.

Student: I don't mind repetitive work. I'm patient, and I really want to learn more about genetics before I apply to graduate school.

Professor: Good. We also have a weekly journal club where everyone presents a recent paper. Would you be comfortable with that?

Student: I think so. I've presented in class before. When can I start?

Professor: How about next Monday? But first, send me your transcript and a short paragraph about why you want to join. I'll email you the details.

Student: Great, I'll do that today. Thank you, Professor.

choices.label: A
choices.text: To ask for a letter of recommendation for graduate school.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To request to join a professor's research project.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To complain about the workload of a biology course.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To discuss the results of a DNA extraction experiment.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lab will be closed for maintenance.

questions.explanation: 考点：推断题。教授说“the first few weeks are mostly repetitive lab work—pipetting, centrifuging, that sort of thing.”，暗示工作可能枯燥但必要。A项与原文相反；C项未提及；D项未提及。

questions.question: What is the student required to do before starting the project?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Attend a summer workshop on DNA extraction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Present a paper at the weekly journal club.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Send his transcript and a short paragraph.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Complete all his required courses.

questions.explanation: 考点：细节题。教授明确说“send me your transcript and a short paragraph about why you want to join.”。A项学生已参加过，不是加入前的要求；B项是加入后每周的活动；D项学生已完成，但并非教授提出的要求。

title: Requesting a Deferred Exam
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a university administrative officer.

Student: Hi, I’m here to request a deferred exam for my biology midterm. I’ve been really sick and couldn’t take it last week.

Officer: I’m sorry to hear that. You’ll need to fill out this form and provide a doctor’s note. The note must state that you were unable to take the exam on the scheduled date.

Student: I have it right here. But I’m worried because the deferred exam is usually scheduled during the last week of the semester, and I already have three other finals that week.

Officer: That is a busy time. However, the deferred exam date is fixed by the university. You can’t change it. But you might talk to your professor about an alternative arrangement, though it’s not guaranteed.

Student: I see. And what about the format? Will it be the same as the original exam?

Officer: Usually yes, but it’s up to the instructor. Some professors give an oral exam or a different version.

Student: Okay. So I just submit this form with the note, and then I wait?

Officer: Exactly. You’ll get a confirmation email within two business days. If you don’t, follow up with our office. Also, make sure you keep a copy of everything for your records.

Student: Thanks for the help. I’ll do that.
