title: Transferring Credits and the Core Curriculum Petition
passage: Student: Professor Alvarez, do you have a minute? I'm Maya Chen, from your Intro to Environmental Policy class last fall. I'm trying to transfer in a course from my old college, and the registrar says I need a faculty signature on this petition. Professor: Sure, have a seat. What's the course? Student: It's called 'Sustainable Cities.' It was a 300-level course, and I basically wrote a policy memo for the final project—twenty pages, with a cost-benefit analysis and everything. I think it's pretty close to your Environmental Policy 301. Professor: Hmm. I remember 301. Let me see the syllabus. Student: Here. The problem is the registrar flagged it as a 'general elective,' not a core requirement, and I'm a senior. If it doesn't count toward the core, I'd have to take an extra class next semester. Professor: I see. The sticking point here is the policy memo. You did the memo, but did you do the simulation exercise? That's the core of 301—students role-play as stakeholders and negotiate a city budget. Student: We didn't. Actually, my professor lectured most of the time. We had one group presentation, but it wasn't a simulation. Professor: That's the issue. The content overlaps, but the skill set is different. I can't just waive the whole thing. Student: So I'm stuck? Professor: Not necessarily. I can approve it as a substitute if you complete a make-up simulation. I run one every semester for transfer students. It's two Saturday sessions, plus a short reflection paper. Student: Two Saturdays? I work weekends. Professor: It's once a semester, and the next one is in October. If you miss it, you'd have to wait until spring—which, as a senior, you probably can't afford. Student: Okay, I'll figure out the work thing. Where do I sign?

title: Career Planning Conversation with an Alumna
passage:
Student: Hi, Ms. Carter. Thanks for meeting with me. I know you're busy as an alumna volunteer.
Alumna: Of course. I remember being in your shoes. What's on your mind?
Student: I'm a junior in environmental science, but I'm torn between grad school and a job in sustainability consulting. Everyone says I need a master's, but I'm not sure.
Alumna: Well, I went straight into consulting after my bachelor's. I learned more in six months on the job than in two years of classes. But later, my firm paid for my master's part-time.
Student: That's interesting. So you didn't need the degree upfront?
Alumna: Not for consulting. But if you want to do research or policy, a graduate degree helps. What draws you to consulting?
Student: I like solving real problems for companies. But I'm worried I'll miss the technical depth.
Alumna: You can always go back to school. I'd suggest applying to a few jobs and one or two master's programs. Then compare offers and funding.
Student: That makes sense. Should I also do an internship this summer?
Alumna: Absolutely. Employers value experience. And it'll help you decide if consulting is right for you.
Student: Thanks. I feel less stressed already.

title: Buying a Textbook at the Campus Bookstore
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a bookstore employee.

Student: Hi, I'm looking for a textbook for my biology class. It's called 'Principles of Genetics,' I think.

Employee: Let me check. Oh, we have a few copies left. Is it for Bio 201?

Student: Yeah, that's the one. How much is it?

Employee: The new copy is $120. But we also have a used copy for $85.

Student: Ouch. That's still a lot. Do you have any rental options?

Employee: Actually, we do. You can rent it for the semester for $45. But you have to return it by the last day of finals.

Student: That sounds better. But what if I want to keep it for reference later?

Employee: Then you might want to buy the used one. It's in good condition, and you can sell it back at the end of the semester for about half the price.

Student: Hmm, let me think. I'll go with the rental. I don't think I'll need it after this class.

Employee: Great. Just need your student ID and you can pick it up at the counter.

Student: Here you go. Thanks!

choices.label: B

title: Discussion with Teaching Assistant About a Research Paper
passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Lee? I'm sorry to bother you during office hours, but I'm a bit confused about the upcoming research paper for your history seminar.

Professor: Oh, hi, Mark. Come on in. What's on your mind?

Student: Well, I've been reading the assignment sheet, and it says we need to use at least five primary sources. But I'm not sure what counts as a primary source for this topic. I'm thinking of writing about the Industrial Revolution in Britain.

Professor: Good topic. Primary sources are original materials from the time period you're studying. So for the Industrial Revolution, things like factory records, government reports, letters, diaries, newspaper articles from that era. Not textbooks or later scholarly articles.

Student: Okay, that makes sense. So a modern documentary would not count?

Professor: Exactly. That would be a secondary source. But you can use secondary sources to support your arguments, just not as one of the five primary ones.

Student: Got it. And one more thing: the paper is due in three weeks, but I have two other major assignments. Could I possibly get an extension?

Professor: I usually don't grant extensions unless there's a real emergency. But you can submit a draft early for feedback. That might help you manage your time better.

Student: That's a great idea. I'll send you a draft by next Friday then.

Professor: Sounds good. See you then.

questions.question: What is the main reason the student visits the professor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To ask for a deadline extension for his paper.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To clarify what qualifies as a primary source for his research paper.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To complain about the difficulty of the assignment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To discuss a documentary he watched about the Industrial Revolution.

questions.explanation: 考点：主旨题。学生一开始就说对研究论文的要求感到困惑，特别是关于一手资料的定义。虽然他也提到了延期，但那是次要问题（后来才提出），而且教授没有同意。A是干扰项，因为延期只是对话的一部分，并非主要目的。C和D在文中没有依据。

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

questions.explanation: 考点：细节题。教授明确说一手资料是来自研究时期的原始材料，比如工厂记录、政府报告、信件、日记、当时的报纸文章，而现代学术文章是二手资料。因此C（2020年发表的学术文章）不属于一手资料。A、B、D都是教授列举的例子。

questions.explanation: 考点：推断题。教授说通常不会批准延期，除非有真正的紧急情况，但她建议学生提前提交草稿以获得反馈，从而更好地管理时间。这暗示她很少给延期，但提供了替代方案。A错误，因为她没有同意延期，只是建议提前交草稿。B和D在文中没有依据。

title: Library Research Consultation for a Paper
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a librarian.

Student: Hi, I'm working on a paper about the effects of urban green spaces on mental health. I've been searching the library database but I'm overwhelmed by the number of results. Could you help me narrow it down?

Librarian: Absolutely. What's your specific angle? Are you looking at physiological effects, like cortisol levels, or more psychological, like stress reduction?

Student: I'm focusing on psychological outcomes—specifically, how community gardens affect residents' sense of belonging and anxiety.

Librarian: That's a great focus. I'd recommend using the subject terms "community gardens" AND "mental health" AND "belonging." Also, limit to peer-reviewed articles from the last ten years. That should give you about thirty to forty relevant studies instead of thousands.

Student: That helps a lot. But I also need some background on the history of urban green spaces in the U.S. Where should I look?

Librarian: For historical context, try books rather than journal articles. We have a good collection on urban planning history. I'll show you the call number range. Also, I noticed you have a lot of search results from non-academic sources. For a research paper, you'll want to filter those out.

Student: Right, I'll do that. Thanks so much!

title: Course Registration Advising Session

title: Revising a Paper at the Writing Center
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a writing center tutor.

Student: Hi, I'm here for my 3 o'clock appointment. I'm working on a paper for my sociology class, and I'm really stuck on the revision.

Tutor: Sure, have a seat. Can you tell me a bit about the assignment?

Student: It's an analysis of urban housing policies. The professor said we need to revise our first draft based on peer feedback. My peers said my thesis is too vague and my evidence is all over the place.

Tutor: Okay. Let's look at your thesis first. Can you read it to me?

Student: "Housing policies have changed over time and affect many people."

Tutor: Hmm, that's a bit broad. What specific change or effect do you want to argue?

Student: Well, I think the 1990s shift to mixed-income developments actually reduced affordable housing in some cities, even though it was supposed to help.

Tutor: That's a strong, arguable claim. Let's use that as your thesis. Now, about your evidence—what sources are you using?

Student: I have some government reports and a couple of news articles. But my peer said I need more academic sources.

Tutor: Yes, for a sociology paper, you should include peer-reviewed studies. Also, make sure each paragraph connects back to your thesis. Let's outline your main points together.

Student: That sounds great. I have about 30 minutes before my next class.

Tutor: Perfect. We can start by reorganizing your arguments from strongest to weakest.

Student: Thanks. I feel much better already.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the conversation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To discuss how to revise a sociology paper.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To complain about a peer's feedback.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To schedule a new appointment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To explain the requirements of a sociology course.

questions.explanation: 考点：主旨。对话围绕学生到写作中心寻求如何修改社会学论文的建议展开， tutor 帮助修改论点、证据和结构，因此 A 正确。B 抱怨同伴反馈只是开头提到的背景，不是目的；C 预约已定，无需再约；D 解释课程要求只是附带信息，不是主要目的。

choices.label: B
choices.text: It needs to include peer-reviewed studies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is sufficient for a sociology paper.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It should focus only on government reports.

questions.explanation: 考点：细节。tutor 明确说“for a sociology paper, you should include peer-reviewed studies”，因此 B 正确。A 与原文相反，学生已有新闻文章，tutor 建议增加学术来源；C 错误，tutor 认为证据需要加强；D 过于绝对，tutor 并未说只用政府报告。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the student's original thesis statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It was too specific and detailed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It was already strong and arguable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It lacked a clear argument.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It focused too much on mixed-income developments.

questions.explanation: 考点：推断。学生原论点“Housing policies have changed over time and affect many people”过于宽泛，tutor 说“that's a bit broad”，并追问具体要论证什么，可见原论点缺乏明确立场。A 相反，是太宽泛而非太具体；B 错误，tutor 认为修改后的新论点才强有力；D 错误，原论点根本没提到 mixed-income developments。

title: IT Service Desk: Laptop Repair Request
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a university IT technician.

title: Ordering the Right Edition

Oh, that's probably because we're between editions. The second edition just sold out, and the third edition isn't in stock yet. It's supposed to arrive next Monday. Are you sure you need the third edition? Some professors say either edition is fine.

Well, my syllabus says third edition, and the professor mentioned that the chapters are reorganized. I'd rather not risk it. But I have a problem: our first assignment is due in two weeks, and I need the book before then.

I understand. We can special-order it for you. It usually takes three to five business days. If you order today, it should be here by Friday. You'd just need to pay a small deposit.

That sounds good. But what about the access code for the online homework platform? I heard it only comes with the new edition.

Right, the third edition includes a one-time access code. If you buy a used copy, the code might already be used. So I'd recommend the new one. The total with tax will be $120.

Okay, let's do the special order. Can I pay the deposit with a card?

Sure. Just fill out this form, and we'll call you when it arrives.

title: Visa Status and Course Registration
passage:
Hi, I'm here to see the international student advisor. My name is Priya Sharma. 

Advisor: Come in, Priya. What can I do for you?

Student: I'm worried about my visa. I'm an F-1 student, and I just realized my I-20 form expired last month. I didn't notice because I was busy with finals. Now I need to register for fall classes, but the system won't let me. 

Advisor: That's a serious issue. You must have a valid I-20 to maintain your F-1 status. Did you apply for an extension before it expired?

Student: No, I didn't. I thought it was automatically renewed since I'm still enrolled.

Advisor: Unfortunately, it's not automatic. You need to submit a new I-20 request with proof of financial support and your academic advisor's signature. Also, since you're out of status, you might need to apply for reinstatement with USCIS. That can take months.

Student: Months? But I have to register for classes next week. What should I do?

Advisor: First, I'll help you file the I-20 extension today. Then you can register for classes while your reinstatement is pending, but you can't work on campus until it's approved. Also, you should talk to your professors about possibly missing the first week if there are delays.

Student: Okay, I'll do that. Thank you for explaining. I had no idea this was so complicated.

title: Finding Sources for a Research Paper
passage:
Student: Hi, I'm working on a paper about the history of the bicycle, and I need to find some primary sources. I've been searching the library catalog but I'm not sure where to start.
Librarian: Sure, I can help. What kind of primary sources are you looking for?
Student: Well, maybe newspaper articles from the late 1800s, or advertisements. I want to see how bicycles were marketed back then.
Librarian: That's a great topic. We have a database called 'Historical Newspapers' that includes articles from major newspapers from 1850 to 1920. You can access it from any computer on campus. Also, we have a special collection of vintage advertisements on microfilm. But you'll need to request them at the reference desk.

Librarian: Not too bad. I can show you how to use the reader. Also, keep in mind that you can't check out microfilm; you'll have to view it here in the library.
Student: Okay, that's good to know. What about secondary sources? I need some scholarly articles too.
Librarian: For those, try the database 'Academic Search Premier.' You can filter by peer-reviewed journals. If you need help with search terms, just let me know.
Student: Thanks, I'll start with the newspaper database first.

title: Course Registration Inquiry at the Registrar's Office

Student: Hi, I'm a sophomore and I'm trying to register for next semester's courses, but the online system keeps saying I need a permission number for Biology 201. I thought I met all the prerequisites.

Student: Great, thanks! Also, I'm thinking about adding a minor in Environmental Studies. Is there a form I need?

title: Financial Aid Application Workshop
passage: Hey, thanks for coming to the financial aid workshop. I know it's a busy time, so let's jump right in. title: Internship Advising Session

Student: Hi, Professor Martinez. Thanks for seeing me on short notice. I'm really interested in doing an internship this summer, but I'm not sure where to start.

Advisor: Ah, that narrows it down. Actually, the biology department runs a summer program with the state parks service. Students work on trail restoration and wildlife monitoring. It's unpaid, but you can earn academic credit.

Student: That sounds perfect. Is there an application deadline?

Advisor: Yes, the priority deadline is March 15th. After that, they only consider applications if spots remain. Also, you'll need a recommendation letter from a faculty member.

Student: Got it. I'll ask Professor Chen. She knows my work in the ecology lab.

Advisor: Good choice. And I'd suggest drafting a resume this week. You can bring it to me for feedback before you submit.

Student: I will. Thanks so much for your help!

title: Transfer Credits Evaluation
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a university admissions advisor.

Student: Hi, I'm here to talk about transferring my credits from my previous college. I've been accepted to the computer science program here, but I'm worried about how many of my credits will actually transfer.

Advisor: Congratulations on your acceptance! Let's take a look. Can you tell me which institution you attended and what courses you took?

Student: I went to Greenfield Community College for two years. I took Calculus I, Introduction to Programming, Data Structures, English Composition, and a few electives like Art History and Psychology.

Advisor: Okay, I have your transcript here. Generally, we accept courses with a grade of C or better that are comparable to our curriculum. Calculus I and Introduction to Programming should transfer directly. Data Structures might not, because our version includes a lab component that yours didn't have.

Student: Oh, that's a problem. Data Structures is a key course for my major. Is there any way to get it approved?

Advisor: You could submit a syllabus from that course for a more detailed review. Sometimes we allow students to take a proficiency exam if the content is similar. But I can't guarantee it.

Student: I see. What about my English Composition? I heard that sometimes writing courses don't transfer.

Advisor: Actually, English Composition usually transfers if it's from an accredited institution. Yours should be fine. The electives, like Art History and Psychology, will likely count as general education credits, but they might not fulfill specific requirements.

Student: Okay. So what's the next step?

Advisor: I'll send you an email with the list of courses that need further evaluation. You can then gather the syllabi and submit them by the end of next week. After that, we'll notify you of the final decision within ten business days.

Student: Great, thanks for your help.

title: Meeting with Teaching Assistant About a Research Paper
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a teaching assistant.

Student: Hi, Professor Lee. Do you have a minute? I'm having trouble with the research paper for your course.

TA: Actually, I'm the teaching assistant, not the professor. But I can help. What's the issue?

Student: Oh, sorry. The assignment says to analyze a case study, but I can't find one that fits the topic. I've looked through the library databases, but everything seems too broad.

TA: I see. Have you tried narrowing your focus? For example, instead of 'climate change policy,' try 'carbon tax implementation in Sweden.' That way, you'll find more specific case studies.

Student: That makes sense. But what about the theoretical framework? I'm not sure which one to use.

TA: You can choose any relevant theory. Just make sure it connects to your case. The rubric doesn't require a specific one. Also, remember the paper is due next Friday, not this Friday. So you have an extra week.

Student: Oh, I thought it was due tomorrow. That's a relief. Thanks for your help!

TA: No problem. If you need more guidance, come to my office hours on Tuesday.

title: Meeting with a Professor About a Presentation
passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Adams. Do you have a minute? I wanted to talk about my presentation for next week's environmental science class.
Professor: Of course, come in. You're presenting on urban gardening, right?
Student: Yes. I've got most of the research done, but I'm not sure how to organize it. I have too much material, and I don't want to bore everyone.
Professor: That's a common problem. What's your main argument?
Student: That urban gardens can improve food access in low-income neighborhoods. But I also found data on air quality, community building, and even crime reduction. I don't want to leave anything out.
Professor: You can't cover everything in ten minutes. Pick two or three key benefits and go deep. For example, focus on food access and community building. Use the air quality data as a quick supporting point.
Student: That makes sense. Should I use slides?
Professor: Yes, but keep them simple. One idea per slide, and don't read from them. Also, practice your timing. Ten minutes goes fast.
Student: Okay. I'll cut the crime data and add a short personal story from the community garden I visited.
Professor: That sounds great. A story will make it memorable. Send me your outline by Friday, and I'll give you feedback.

title: Office Hours: Refining a Research Paper
passage:
Professor: Come in, Alex. How's the research paper coming along?
Student: Well, I've hit a bit of a wall. I have all these sources on urban gardening, but I'm not sure how to organize them into a coherent argument.
Professor: Let's take a look at your outline. I see you've listed a lot of benefits—community building, food access, environmental impact. But what's your thesis?
Student: I guess I don't really have one yet. I just wanted to show that urban gardens are good.
Professor: That's too broad. A strong paper needs a debatable claim. For example, you could argue that urban gardens are more effective at building social cohesion than at improving food security, and then support that with evidence.
Student: Oh, I see. So I need to take a position and defend it.
Professor: Exactly. Also, your sources are mostly from the past five years, which is great, but you're missing some key counterarguments. Have you looked at critics who say urban gardens can lead to gentrification?
Student: No, I haven't. I didn't think of that.
Professor: You should address that. It'll make your paper more balanced. Why don't you revise your thesis and add a section on counterarguments? Bring a draft next week.
Student: That sounds doable. Thanks, Professor.

title: Transfer Credits Meeting

Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a university advisor. 

Student: Hi, Professor Martinez. I'm glad I caught you during office hours. I'm thinking about transferring to the state university next fall, and I need to know how my credits will transfer.

Student: Not yet. I wanted to talk to you first. I've taken about 60 credits here, including general education requirements and some electives. 

Advisor: Okay. Typically, the state university accepts credits from accredited institutions if the courses are comparable and you earned a C or better. But you'll need to submit course descriptions or syllabi for each class you want evaluated. 

Student: That sounds like a lot of work. Is there a limit on how many credits they'll accept? 

Advisor: Yes, they usually cap transfer credits at 90 semester hours. Also, some majors have specific requirements. For example, if you're going into engineering, they might not accept your introductory calculus if it wasn't calculus-based. 

Student: I see. I'm planning to major in psychology, so hopefully most of my courses will count. 

Advisor: Psychology should be fine. But you'll need to check with the department about their residency requirement—usually you have to take at least 30 credits at the new school. 

Student: Got it. So I should start gathering syllabi now? 

Advisor: Exactly. And make sure to meet with an advisor at the state university before you apply, so you know exactly what will transfer. 

Student: Thanks, Professor. I'll do that.

title: Requesting a Dorm Room Change
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a housing officer.

Student: Hi, I'm sorry to bother you. I need to talk about my dorm room. I'm having a really hard time sleeping because my roommate stays up late playing video games with the sound on. I've asked him to use headphones, but he forgets.

Housing Officer: I see. Have you tried talking to your resident advisor?

Student: Yes, I did last week. He suggested I try to work it out directly, but it's not getting better. I'm falling behind in my morning classes because I'm so tired.

Housing Officer: That's not good. Let me check what rooms are available. We have a few singles, but they cost extra. There's also a double in the quiet wing of Building C. Would you be open to that?

Student: A quiet wing sounds perfect. I don't mind having a roommate as long as it's quiet. How much would it cost?

Housing Officer: The quiet wing is the same price as your current room. But I need to confirm with the resident director first. Can you come back tomorrow afternoon?

Student: Sure. What time?

Housing Officer: Anytime after 2 p.m. And bring your student ID.

Student: Will do. Thanks so much!

title: Financial Aid Application Meeting
passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Martinez. Do you have a minute? I'm applying for the summer research grant, and I need a faculty sponsor. I was hoping you might consider it.
Professor: Of course, Lisa. Your work on urban pollinators last semester was impressive. But the deadline is this Friday—have you started the application?
Student: I've drafted the research proposal, but I'm stuck on the budget section. The grant covers up to $3,000, but I'm not sure what counts as eligible expenses.
Professor: Typically, it covers supplies, travel for fieldwork, and a small stipend. It doesn't cover equipment over $500 or conference fees.
Student: That's helpful. I was planning to buy a new microscope, but I guess I'll use the lab's instead.
Professor: Right. Also, you'll need a letter of recommendation from me. I can write it, but I need your proposal by Wednesday so I have time to review it.
Student: Wednesday... I can email it to you by Tuesday night.
Professor: Perfect. And don't forget to submit the online form separately—the department won't process your application without it.
Student: I'll do that right after this. Thanks so much, Professor!

choices.label: B

passage:
Hi, I'm looking for the textbook for Introduction to Environmental Science. The course code is ENV 101. Do you have it in stock?

Let me check... Yes, we have a few copies left. But just so you know, we only have the loose-leaf edition. The hardcover version sold out last week.

Oh, that's fine. How much is the loose-leaf?

It's $85. But if you buy the loose-leaf, you'll also need a binder. We sell those for $10.

Okay, I'll take both. Also, I noticed a sign about a buyback program. Can I sell my old books here?

Absolutely. We buy back books during the last two weeks of the semester. Just bring your student ID and the books. We'll assess their condition and make an offer. But keep in mind, we only buy back books that are currently being used for courses next semester.

Got it. And do you price match with online retailers?

Sorry, we don't. Our prices are set by the publisher, and we can't change them.

That's okay. I'll just get the loose-leaf and binder for now. Do you accept credit cards?

Yes, we do. But there's a minimum purchase of $5 for card payments, which you've met.

Great. Here's my card.

title: Meeting with a Teaching Assistant About a Lab Report
passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Chen. Do you have a minute?
TA: Actually, I'm the teaching assistant for this course. Professor Chen is only here on Tuesdays. How can I help you?
Student: Oh, sorry. I'm having trouble with the lab report that's due next Friday. I don't understand what we're supposed to write in the discussion section.
TA: Let's see. You need to interpret your results and compare them with your hypothesis. Did you collect all the data?
Student: Yes, but my results don't match the hypothesis at all. I'm worried I did something wrong.
TA: That happens in science. Your job is to explain why the results might differ. For example, did you control the temperature? Any unexpected variables?
Student: I didn't think about that. The lab was pretty warm that day.
TA: Exactly. Mention that in the discussion. Also, you should cite at least two sources to support your explanation.
Student: Okay. So I don't need to redo the experiment?
TA: No, not unless there was a major error. Just analyze the results you have. And remember, the report is due Friday at 5 p.m. You can submit it online.
Student: Got it. Thanks for your help!

choices.label: B

choices.text: Complain about the lab equipment.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ignore the results and write about the hypothesis instead.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Explain possible reasons for the discrepancy in the discussion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ask another student to share their data.

questions.explanation: 细节题。助教说‘Your job is to explain why the results might differ’，并建议提到温度等变量，因此C正确。A与助教明确说的‘No, not unless there was a major error’矛盾；B、D未提及。

title: Visa Renewal Crisis
passage:
Listen to a conversation between a student and an international student advisor.

Student: Hi, I'm here because my student visa expires next month, and I'm not sure what to do. I need to renew it, but I heard it might take a long time.

Advisor: Right, it can take several weeks. Have you started the renewal process?

Student: No, I just realized my visa expires on the 15th of next month. I'm worried because I have a conference to attend in two months, and I need a valid visa to travel.

Advisor: That's tight. You should apply for renewal as soon as possible. But first, make sure your I-20 is up to date and you have all the required documents.

Student: I think my I-20 is fine, but I haven't checked. What documents do I need?

Advisor: You'll need a valid passport, your I-20, a photo, and the application fee. Also, you might need to provide proof of financial support.

Student: Okay. Do I need to leave the country to renew?

Advisor: Not necessarily. If you're eligible for automatic visa revalidation, you can renew while staying here, but that depends on your situation. Actually, for renewals, you usually have to apply at a U.S. embassy or consulate abroad. But wait, there's a exception: if you're traveling to Canada or Mexico for less than 30 days, you might be able to re-enter with an expired visa, but that's not renewal.

Student: So I have to go back to my home country to renew?

Advisor: Possibly, but check with the embassy. Some countries allow third-country nationals to renew. However, given your timeline, you might want to consider expedited processing.

Student: I see. I'll start right away. Thanks!

questions.question: What is the main problem the student is facing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His student visa will expire soon and he needs to renew it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He lost his passport and cannot travel.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He missed his conference because of visa issues.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He does not have enough money to pay the application fee.

questions.explanation: 考点：主旨。学生一开始就说明学生签证下个月到期，需要续签，所以A正确。B护照丢失未提及；C会议是未来要参加，不是错过了；D费用问题未提及。

choices.label: B

choices.label: D
choices.text: A health insurance certificate.

questions.explanation: 考点：细节。顾问提到需要有效护照、I-20、照片、申请费以及可能需要的资金证明，所以B正确。A、C、D均未提及。

choices.label: B
choices.text: He must travel to Canada or Mexico to renew his visa.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He might need to return to his home country to renew his visa.

title: Hotel Room Booking Inquiry
passage:
Good morning, thanks for calling the Grand Plaza Hotel. How can I help you?  
Hi, I'd like to book a room for next weekend, from Friday the 14th to Sunday the 16th.  
Certainly. We have double rooms and twin rooms available. Which would you prefer?  
A double room, please. Is breakfast included?  
Yes, a full English breakfast is included in the rate. It's served from 7 to 10 a.m. in the dining room.  
Great. How much is the room per night?  
It's £90 per night, but if you stay two nights, we offer a 10% discount.  
That sounds good. Does the room have a view?  
We can offer a room overlooking the garden or the car park. The garden view is slightly more expensive, an extra £10 per night.  
I'll take the garden view, please.  
Alright. Can I have your name and a contact number?  
Yes, it's Sarah Mitchell, and my mobile is 07700 900123.  
Thank you, Ms. Mitchell. We look forward to seeing you on the 14th.

title: Opening a Student Bank Account
passage:
WOMAN: Good morning, how can I help you?
MAN: Hi, I'd like to open a student bank account, please.
WOMAN: Certainly. Are you a full-time student at the university here?
MAN: Yes, I'm in my first year, studying engineering.
WOMAN: Great. Could I see your passport and your student ID card, please?
MAN: Here's my passport. But I don't have my student ID yet — I only enrolled last week.
WOMAN: That's fine. I can accept your offer letter instead. Do you have that with you?
MAN: Yes, I do. Here it is.
WOMAN: Thank you. Now, do you want just a current account, or would you like a savings account as well?
MAN: Just a current account for now. I might add savings later.
WOMAN: No problem. There's no monthly fee for students. You'll get a debit card, which usually arrives within five working days. Would you like online banking set up today?
MAN: Yes, please. That would be really handy.
WOMAN: Alright. I'll just need you to create a password and a memorable word. Also, please note that the daily withdrawal limit is two hundred pounds.
MAN: Two hundred? That's a bit low. Can I increase it?
WOMAN: Yes, you can request a higher limit after three months. Now, let me take a few more details...

title: Phone Repair Shop Conversation

I see. What model is it?

Okay. For the screen replacement, it'll be £120, and a new battery is £45. If you want both, we can do a discount—£150 total.

That sounds reasonable. How long will it take?

Usually 2 to 3 working days. But if you need it urgently, we offer a same-day service for an extra £20. However, that depends on whether we have the parts in stock. Let me check... Yes, we do have the screen and battery for the S21 right now.

Great. I'll go with the same-day service then. What do I need to do?

Just leave your phone here and fill in this form with your name, contact number, and a description of the problem. We'll call you when it's ready. Also, please back up your data before you come—we're not responsible for data loss.

Okay, I'll back it up tonight and bring it in tomorrow morning.

Perfect. We open at 9 a.m.

title: Insurance Inquiry Call
passage:
Woman: Good morning. I'm calling about the home insurance quote I requested online. My name's Sarah Mitchell.

Man: Certainly, Ms. Mitchell. I've got your details here. You're looking at our standard contents and buildings policy for a two-bedroom flat in Brighton, is that right?

Woman: That's correct. But I noticed the online quote was £42 a month. Is that the final price?

Man: It depends. That quote assumes a £250 excess. If you raise the excess to £500, the monthly premium drops to £35. And if you're over 60, there's a 10% discount, but I see you're 34, so that won't apply.

Woman: I see. Can I add accidental damage cover?

Man: Yes, that's an extra £6 per month. It covers things like spilling wine on a carpet or dropping your laptop.

Woman: What about my bicycle? It's worth about £800. Is it covered automatically?

Man: Only up to £300 under the standard policy. To cover the full value, you'd need the 'Valuables Plus' add-on, which is £4 a month.

Woman: Okay. And how soon can the policy start?

Man: Once you pay, cover begins at midnight the same day. But if you want it active immediately, there's a £15 express fee.

Woman: Let's just go with midnight. I'll confirm by email this afternoon.

Man: Perfect. I'll send the documents now.

title: Calling a Moving Company

W: Good morning, Swift Movers. How can I help you?
M: Hi, I need to book a moving service. I'm moving from a two-bedroom apartment to a house about 20 miles away.
W: Sure. When would you like us to move you?

M: The morning is better. I want to get it done early.
W: Great. Now, how much furniture do you have? Any large items like a piano or a safe?
M: No piano, but we do have a large sofa, a dining table, and a refrigerator. Oh, and about 20 boxes.
W: Okay. Our rate is £40 per hour for a two-man team, plus a £30 call-out fee. It usually takes about 4 to 5 hours for a two-bedroom move.
M: That sounds reasonable. Do you provide packing materials?
W: Yes, we sell boxes and tape, but you can also use your own. We recommend double-walled boxes for books.
M: I'll keep that in mind. Can I pay by card on the day?
W: Of course. We just need a £50 deposit to secure the booking. Would you like to go ahead?

title: Visa Application Enquiry
passage:
W: Good morning. I'd like to ask about applying for a visitor visa to Canada. My sister is getting married in Vancouver next June, and I plan to stay for three weeks. Could you tell me what documents I need?
M: Certainly. You'll need a valid passport, a completed application form, two recent passport-sized photos, and proof of funds — like a bank statement from the last six months. Have you booked your flights yet?
W: Not yet. I was told it's better to wait until the visa is approved. Is that correct?
M: Yes, that's usually recommended. Also, do you have travel insurance? It's not mandatory for a visitor visa, but it's strongly advised.
W: I see. And how long does the process take?
M: Normally about four to six weeks, but during peak seasons it can take up to eight weeks. So I'd suggest applying at least three months before your trip.
W: That's helpful. One more thing — do I need to attend an interview?
M: Not for a visitor visa, unless your case is flagged for further review. If that happens, you'll be contacted by email.
W: Great. Could I also get a checklist of all the documents?
M: Of course. I'll email it to you this afternoon. Just write your email address on this form.

title: Courier Service Phone Conversation

WOMAN: Good morning, SwiftCourier. How can I help you?

MAN: OK. And how can I track it?

WOMAN: You'll get a tracking number via email once it's scanned. You can track it on our website or app.

MAN: Thanks. That's all I needed.

Actually, I'm quite interested. But I have a small doorway – will the sofa fit? I'm worried about getting it inside.

Good question. The sofa comes in two pieces and the legs can be removed, so it fits through most standard doors. Our delivery team can also assemble it for you at no extra cost.

That's reassuring. Can I pay a deposit to hold it until the weekend?

Yes, a 20% deposit secures it for seven days. You can pay over the phone or in store.

Great. I'll come in tomorrow with my card.

Perfect. I'll make a note of your name and number, and we'll hold the sofa for you.

title: IELTS Visa Application Phone Call
passage:
Good morning, Visa Application Centre. How can I help you?

Oh, hello. I'd like to apply for a student visa to the UK. Can you tell me what documents I need to bring?

Certainly. You'll need your passport, a completed application form, two recent passport-sized photos, and your letter of acceptance from the university. Also, you must provide proof of funds to show you can cover your tuition and living costs.

Right. Do I need to show bank statements?

Yes. Bank statements for the last six months. If the account is in your parents' name, you'll also need a letter from them confirming they'll support you financially.

Okay. And what about the visa fee?

It's 348 pounds for a standard student visa. You can pay by credit card or debit card at the centre. We don't accept cash.

How long does the process usually take?

Usually about three weeks, but during peak season it can take up to six weeks. So I'd advise you to apply as early as possible.

Can I book an appointment online?

Yes, just go to our website and choose a date and time. You'll need to bring your appointment confirmation when you come.

Great. One more thing—do I need to attend an interview?

Not always, but some applicants are asked to come for a short interview. We'll inform you by email if that's the case.

Thank you very much. You've been very helpful.

You're welcome. Good luck with your application.

title: Post Office Parcel Delivery Conversation

A: Good morning, welcome to City Express Post. How can I help you today?
B: Hi, I need to send a parcel to Manchester. It's a birthday gift for my sister.
A: Sure. Could you place it on the scale, please? ... Okay, it weighs 3.2 kilograms. When would you like it to arrive?
B: Ideally by this Friday. Her birthday is on Saturday.
A: Our standard delivery takes 3 to 5 working days, so it might not arrive until next Monday. If you want it there by Friday, I'd recommend our express service. It guarantees next-day delivery if posted before 4 p.m.
B: That sounds better. How much is express?
A: For a 3.2 kg parcel to Manchester, express is £12.50. Standard is £7.20.
B: Okay, I'll go with express. Can I also add insurance? The gift is quite valuable.
A: Yes, insurance up to £50 is included free. Additional coverage up to £500 costs £3.50. Would you like that?
B: Yes, please. And could you pack it for me? I'm worried about damage.
A: Of course. Packing service is £2.00. So your total comes to £18.00. Please fill in this form with the recipient's address and your contact details.
B: Alright. Do you need a phone number?
A: Yes, both yours and the recipient's, in case of delivery issues.

title: Restaurant Booking for a Birthday Dinner
passage:
WOMAN: Good morning, Bella Vista Restaurant. How can I help you?
MAN: Hi, I'd like to book a table for this Saturday evening. It's my wife's birthday, so something a bit special.
WOMAN: Of course. How many people will it be?
MAN: Let me think – there's the two of us, plus our daughter and her husband, and my wife's parents. So that's six.

WOMAN: I'll put a note on the booking, but I can't guarantee it – Saturdays are busy.

WOMAN: Could you spell that for me?
MAN: A-T-K-I-N-S-O-N.
WOMAN: Got it. And a phone number?
MAN: 07700 900 234.
WOMAN: Perfect. So that's Saturday the 14th at 7:30, for six people, under Atkinson. We'll see you then.

title: Inquiring About House Cleaning Services

title: Welcome to Bramble Park: A Guided Introduction
passage:
Hello and welcome to Bramble Park! I'm Sarah, your guide for today. Before we start our walk, let me give you a quick overview of the park and its facilities.

Bramble Park was established in 1923 and covers about 45 acres. It's known for its rare collection of oak trees, some over 300 years old. The park is divided into three main areas: the Rose Garden, the Woodland Trail, and the Lakeside Meadow.

The Rose Garden is closest to the entrance and is at its best in early summer. Just beyond it, you'll find the Woodland Trail, a 2-mile loop that's popular with joggers. The Lakeside Meadow is a bit further, about a 15-minute walk from here. It's a great spot for picnics, and you can often see swans and ducks there.

A few practical points: the park is open from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. daily. There's a café near the main entrance that serves light snacks and drinks. Restrooms are located next to the café and also near the Lakeside Meadow. Bicycles are not allowed on the Woodland Trail, but you can cycle on the main paths.

Finally, if you're interested in joining a guided tour, we offer them every Saturday at 10 a.m. and 2 p.m. The tours last about 90 minutes and are free of charge. Just sign up at the visitor center.

Alright, let's begin our walk. Please stay together and follow me.

title: Belfast City Hall Tour Information
passage:
Hello everyone, and welcome to Belfast City Hall. I'm your guide, and before we begin today's tour, let me give you some practical information to help you make the most of your visit. 

First, a bit of history. City Hall opened in 1906 and is one of Belfast's most iconic buildings. The interior is made of Italian marble, and the stained-glass windows tell stories from the city's past. 

Now, about the tour. The guided tour lasts about 45 minutes and takes you through the main entrance, the Grand Hall, and the council chamber. Photography is allowed inside, but please don't use flash in the council chamber, as it can damage the old paintings. 

If you'd like to explore on your own, we also offer a free audio guide in eight languages, available at the reception desk. The building is open to the public from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays, and from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekends. 

One more thing—the Bobbin Coffee Shop on the ground floor is a lovely spot for lunch, but it gets very busy around noon. I'd recommend going before 12 or after 2 if you want a table. 

Finally, don't forget to visit the grounds outside. The gardens are particularly beautiful in spring, and the Titanic Memorial is just a short walk away. 

Are there any questions before we start?

title: Understanding and Managing Sleep Cycles
passage:
Good morning everyone. Thank you for coming to today's health talk. I'm Dr. Claire Bennett, and I'm here to discuss something we all do but often overlook: sleep. 

Many people think sleep is just a time when the body shuts down. But actually, it's a highly active state. During the night, we cycle through different stages—light sleep, deep sleep, and what's called REM sleep, where dreaming occurs. Each cycle lasts about 90 minutes, and we typically go through four to six cycles per night. 

Now, a common problem is that people try to catch up on sleep during weekends, thinking it will fix a week of poor rest. Unfortunately, this disrupts your body clock, or circadian rhythm, making Monday mornings even harder. Instead, you should aim for a consistent bedtime and wake-up time, even on weekends. 

Another tip: avoid caffeine after 2 p.m. Caffeine can stay in your system for up to eight hours, so that afternoon coffee might still be keeping you awake at midnight. Also, keep your bedroom cool, dark, and quiet. And finally, if you can't fall asleep within 20 minutes, don't lie there worrying. Get up, do something relaxing like reading, and try again when you feel sleepy.

title: Volunteer Recruitment for the Greenway Community Garden
passage:
Hello, and welcome to the community announcement. I'm Sarah, the volunteer coordinator for the Greenway Community Garden. We're looking for new volunteers to help with our spring planting season. The garden is located behind the public library on Oak Street, and we're open every day from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.

We have three main roles. First, garden assistants help with planting, weeding, and watering. No experience is needed—we'll provide training on your first day. Second, we need welcome desk volunteers to greet visitors, answer questions, and sign up new members. For this role, you need good communication skills and basic computer knowledge. Third, we're looking for event helpers to assist with our monthly workshops, like the composting class on the first Saturday of each month.

Volunteers must be at least 16 years old. You can choose your own hours, but we ask for a minimum of four hours per month. All volunteers receive a free T-shirt, and after 20 hours of service, you'll get a certificate. If you're interested, please fill out the online form on our website, or visit us in person. The deadline to apply is March 15th. Thank you for listening, and we hope to see you in the garden!

title: City Art Museum's New Exhibition: 'Echoes of the Sea'
passage: Welcome to the City Art Museum. I'm your guide for today's tour of our latest exhibition, 'Echoes of the Sea'. This exhibition features over fifty works by contemporary artists from coastal communities around the world. It explores how the ocean has shaped their cultures, livelihoods, and identities. Before we begin, let me give you some practical information. The exhibition is spread across three rooms on the ground floor. Room one focuses on traditional fishing practices, room two on the impact of climate change, and room three on myths and legends of the sea. You are free to explore at your own pace, but I recommend starting in room one to follow the chronological order. Photography is allowed, but please turn off your flash to protect the artworks. Also, note that room two has a short film playing every thirty minutes, starting at ten past the hour. The next showing will be at 2:10. Finally, don't miss the interactive display in room three, where you can create your own digital wave patterns. The exhibition runs until the end of next month. Enjoy your visit!

title: Riverside Fitness Centre: Membership and Facilities
passage:
Hello everyone, and welcome to the Riverside Fitness Centre. I'm your membership coordinator, and I'd like to give you a quick overview of what we offer and how to make the most of your membership.

First, our opening hours. On weekdays, we're open from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. On weekends, we open slightly later, at 8 a.m., but we close at 8 p.m. So if you're an early bird on Saturday, you'll have to wait a bit.

Now, about the facilities. We have a large gym with modern equipment, two swimming pools — one indoor and one outdoor — and a sauna. The outdoor pool is only open during the summer months, from June to August. 

We also offer a wide range of classes, including yoga, spinning, and aqua aerobics. Most classes are free for members, but there's a small fee of three pounds for spinning because of the special bikes. You can book classes through our app or at the front desk.

Finally, a few rules. Please remember to bring your membership card and a towel. Towels are not provided, but you can rent one for one pound. Also, please re-rack your weights after use. 

If you have any questions, feel free to ask me or any of our staff. Enjoy your workout!

title: Community Charity Fun Run
passage:
Hello everyone, and welcome to the community centre. My name's Sarah, and I'm the lead organiser for this year's charity fun run. Now, I know many of you have taken part before, but we've made a few changes, so please listen carefully.

First, the date. It's on Saturday the 15th of June, not the 8th as some posters said. We had to move it because the park is hosting a music festival that weekend.

The route is also different. Instead of the usual 5-kilometre loop around the lake, we're doing a 10-kilometre route that goes through the woods and finishes at the old train station. It's flatter, so it should be easier for families with young children.

Registration is £12 for adults and £6 for under-16s. That includes a T-shirt and a bottle of water. But if you register online before the 1st of June, you get a 20% discount.

Now, about parking. The main car park will be closed for the festival, so please use the Park-and-Ride on Mill Road. Buses run every 15 minutes from 7 a.m.

Finally, we still need volunteers to hand out water at the stations and to help with the finish line. If you can help, please sign up at the desk near the entrance.

Thanks, and we hope to see you there!

title: Riverside Music Festival: Volunteer Briefing
passage: Hello, and thank you for volunteering at this year's Riverside Music Festival. I'm your volunteer coordinator, and I want to quickly run through the key arrangements for the weekend. First, a change from last year: all volunteers must check in at the staff tent, not the main gate. The staff tent is just to the left of the main entrance, next to the lost property office. You'll receive your wristband and a meal voucher there. Now, about shifts. Saturday is our busiest day, so we've had to adjust some timings. If you're on the afternoon shift, please arrive by 12:30, not 1:00 as originally planned. The evening shift starts at 5:00 and finishes at 11:00. On Sunday, we're a bit more relaxed, with two shifts: 10:00 to 4:00, and 4:00 to 10:00. One more important thing — the main stage area gets extremely crowded after 7 p.m., so we ask volunteers to use the backstage route when moving between stages. It's a bit longer, but much safer. Finally, if you have any problems during your shift, don't call the general information line. Instead, contact your team leader directly. Their numbers are on the back of your volunteer badge. Any questions?

title: Community Recycling Initiative
passage: Hello everyone, and welcome to the monthly meeting of the Greenfield Community Association. I'm Sarah, your coordinator, and today I'm excited to tell you about our new recycling initiative called 'Bin It Right'. As you know, our town has struggled with waste management, and last year, we sent over 2,000 tons of recyclable materials to landfill. That's why we've decided to take action. Starting next month, we'll be introducing a simplified system with three colored bins: blue for paper and cardboard, green for glass and metals, and yellow for plastics. But here's the key change: we're asking residents to rinse containers before recycling. Why? Because contaminated items can ruin entire batches of recycling. We'll also be launching a weekly collection schedule: blue and green bins on Tuesdays, and yellow bins on Thursdays. To help you remember, we've created a free mobile app with reminders and a sorting guide. You can download it from our website. Finally, we're looking for volunteers to help spread the word. If you're interested, please sign up at the back table. Together, we can make a real difference.

title: Temporary Traffic Diversion Notice for Riverside Road
passage: Hello, this is a recorded message from the City Council. I'm calling to inform residents about a temporary traffic diversion on Riverside Road starting next Monday, the 15th of May. The road will be closed for essential repairs to a water main, and the work is expected to last for three weeks. During this time, all vehicles will be diverted via Mill Street and Queen's Avenue. This will add approximately ten minutes to your journey, so please allow extra time. Buses on routes 12 and 15 will also be affected. They will not stop at Riverside Park or the Library. Instead, temporary stops will be set up on Mill Street near the post office and on Queen's Avenue opposite the supermarket. Pedestrians and cyclists can still use Riverside Road, but please follow the signed diversions. Access to the Riverside Shopping Centre will remain open from the Queen's Avenue entrance. We apologise for any inconvenience and thank you for your patience. For more information, visit our website or call 0800 123 4567.

title: Evening Course in Practical Bookkeeping
passage:
Hello, and welcome to the Riverside Adult Education Centre. I'm Daniel Hart, and I coordinate the evening vocational courses. I'm going to give you some information about our new Practical Bookkeeping course, which starts on Tuesday the fifth of March.

Now, this course is aimed at people who run small businesses or who handle accounts as part of their job, but who have no formal training. It's not a course for qualified accountants. We'll cover the basics of double-entry bookkeeping, how to prepare a simple profit-and-loss statement, and how to use a spreadsheet to track expenses. We won't be covering tax law, as that's a separate course.

The classes run every Tuesday evening from six thirty to eight thirty, in Room B4 on the first floor. There are twelve sessions in total, and you'll need to bring a calculator and a notebook. The course fee is two hundred and forty pounds, which includes a textbook. If you're unemployed or receiving benefits, you can apply for a reduced fee of one hundred and twenty pounds.

One more thing: the course is very popular, and we only have twenty places. So if you'd like to join, please register online by Friday the first of March. Don't just turn up on the first night, because we can't guarantee a place at the door.

title: Evening Pottery Course Orientation
passage:
Hello everyone, and welcome to the Westbridge Community Centre. My name is Laura Bennett, and I'm the coordinator for our evening adult courses. I'm here to give you a quick orientation for the eight-week pottery course that starts next Monday.

First, let me explain the schedule. Classes run every Monday and Wednesday from 6:30 to 8:30 p.m. in Studio B, which is on the ground floor, just past the main reception desk. Please arrive about ten minutes early on the first day so we can get everyone signed in.

Now, about materials. The course fee of ninety pounds covers clay, glazes, and the use of all our equipment. However, you will need to bring your own apron and a small towel. We do sell aprons at reception for eight pounds if you'd prefer not to bring one.

A word about clothing: please wear something comfortable that you don't mind getting dirty. Pottery is messy work, and clay stains are very hard to remove once they dry.

On the final evening of the course, we'll hold a small exhibition in the main hall. You're welcome to invite family and friends. Each student can display up to three pieces, and there will be light refreshments.

Finally, if you have to miss a class, don't worry. We run a catch-up session on Saturday mornings at ten o'clock, free of charge. Just let me know by Friday if you plan to attend.

Are there any questions before we move on?

title: The History of Bardsley Market
passage: Welcome, everyone, to the Bardsley Heritage Walking Tour. Before we set off, let me give you a quick history of Bardsley Market, which is the oldest part of our town. Most people assume the market began in the fifteenth century, but recent archaeological digs actually date the first stalls to around 1280, when local farmers began trading surplus grain and wool. The market cross you'll see in a moment is not the original — that one was destroyed by fire in 1666, and the current stone cross was erected in 1702. For over three hundred years, the market sold mainly livestock, but that changed in the 1840s when the railway arrived. Fresh produce from surrounding villages could suddenly reach the town within hours, and by 1900 the cattle market had moved to the outskirts, leaving the square for fruit, vegetables, and flowers. One thing that hasn't changed is the tradition of the 'market bell', rung at eight o'clock every Saturday morning to officially open trading. It's been rung, without exception, since 1750 — even during the two world wars. So, if you hear it later this morning, you'll know exactly what it means. Now, please follow me.

title: Welcome to TechnoQuest Science Centre
passage:
Hello everyone, and welcome to TechnoQuest Science Centre. I'm Daniel, your guide for today. Before we start, let me give you a quick overview of what's here and how to make the most of your visit. 

TechnoQuest is divided into four main zones. The first is the Space Zone, where you can try our famous zero-gravity simulator. Please note that this ride has a height restriction: you must be at least 1.4 metres tall. Next is the Robotics Zone, where a new exhibit opens today—a robot that can solve a Rubik's cube in under five seconds. It's already attracting huge crowds, so I'd suggest heading there early if you want a good view. 

The third zone is the Energy Zone, which focuses on renewable power. There, you can pedal a bike to generate electricity and see how long it takes to boil a kettle. Finally, the Nature Zone explores biomimicry—how engineers copy designs from animals. 

A few practical tips: the café on the ground floor gets very busy between twelve and two, so consider eating earlier or later. Also, the gift shop closes at five, half an hour before the centre itself. And if you lose your group, don't worry—we have free Wi-Fi, and you can use our app to track each other's locations. Any questions so far?

title: The Riverside Food and Wine Festival
passage: Hello everyone, and welcome to this short talk about the upcoming Riverside Food and Wine Festival. I'm Emma, the event coordinator, and I'm delighted to give you a preview of what's in store. The festival will take place over the weekend of July 15th and 16th at Riverside Park, right along the riverbank. Gates open at 10 a.m. both days, and the last entry is at 8 p.m. Now, a few practical points. Tickets are twelve pounds per day if you buy in advance online, or fifteen pounds at the gate. Children under twelve get in free, but they must be accompanied by an adult at all times. Once inside, you'll find over forty stalls offering dishes from more than twenty countries. This year we've added a special 'Chef's Corner' where local chefs will give free cooking demonstrations every hour. However, please note that the popular wine-tasting sessions are not included in the entry ticket; they cost an extra eight pounds and must be booked in advance, as places are limited. Also, a quick reminder: no outside food or drinks are allowed, except for baby food and water bottles. We encourage you to bring your own reusable cup to reduce waste. Finally, dogs are welcome, but they must be kept on a lead. We look forward to seeing you there!

title: Volunteer Recruitment Fair Announcement
passage: Good morning everyone, and welcome to the community center. I'm Sarah, the volunteer coordinator, and I'm here to tell you about our upcoming Volunteer Recruitment Fair. This year, the fair will be held on Saturday, September 14th, from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. in the main hall of the Riverside Community Center. We have over thirty local charities and non-profit organizations participating, covering areas like environmental conservation, animal welfare, education, and elderly care. Whether you're interested in hands-on work or behind-the-scenes support, there's something for everyone. Now, a few practical points. Entry is free, but you need to register in advance on our website so we can prepare enough information packs. Each pack includes a map of the stalls, a schedule of short talks, and a list of current volunteer opportunities. Please note that parking at the center is limited, so we strongly encourage you to use public transport. The number 12 bus stops right outside, and the Riverside train station is only a ten-minute walk away. Also, if you have any questions, feel free to visit our info desk near the entrance. We look forward to seeing you there!

title: Welcome to Willowbrook Farm Cottages
passage:
Hello and welcome to Willowbrook Farm Cottages. I'm Sarah, the owner, and I'm here to tell you a bit about what we offer and how to make the most of your stay. We have five self-catering cottages, each sleeping up to four people. They're all named after wildflowers—Bluebell, Foxglove, Heather, Clover, and Daisy. If you're in Bluebell, you'll find it's the closest to the swimming pool, which is heated from April to October. Foxglove and Heather are slightly further back, overlooking the orchard. Clover and Daisy are next to the communal barbecue area, so they're ideal if you like to eat outdoors.

Now, a few practical points. Breakfast baskets can be ordered the night before and are delivered to your door by 7:30 a.m. They include fresh eggs from our hens, homemade bread, and seasonal fruit. There's no extra charge, but we do ask you to let us know by 9 p.m. Wi-Fi is available in all cottages, though the signal is strongest in the main farmhouse. If you need to work, you're welcome to use the study there.

For children, we have a play area with a sandpit and a small climbing frame. And on Saturdays, we run a free tractor ride around the farm at 10 a.m. Finally, please remember that we're a working farm, so for your safety, always close gates behind you and don't enter fields with livestock.

title: Ski Resort Safety Announcement
passage: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Pine Valley Ski Resort. Before you head out to the slopes, I'd like to go over a few important safety reminders and practical tips to ensure you have an enjoyable day. First, please be aware that all skiers and snowboarders must wear a helmet. You can rent one from the equipment rental shop near the main lodge if you don't have your own. Second, always stay on marked trails. The off-piste areas may look tempting, but they are not patrolled and can be dangerous due to hidden rocks and tree wells. Third, check the daily avalanche forecast posted at the bottom of each lift. If the risk is high, certain areas will be closed. Respect all closures and signs. Fourth, when skiing, keep a safe distance from others. The person in front of you has the right of way. Finally, if you witness an accident, do not move the injured person unless they are in immediate danger. Instead, cross your skis in an X above the victim to alert others and call the ski patrol at the number on your ticket. Remember, safety first, and have a great time on the slopes!

title: Astronomy Observatory Open Day
passage:
Hello everyone, and welcome to the Greenfield Observatory Open Day. My name is Dr. Sarah Mitchell, and I'm the lead astronomer here. Before we start the tour, I'd like to give you a quick overview of what you'll see today.

First, we'll visit the main dome, which houses our 1.2-meter reflecting telescope. It's one of the largest in the region, and it's used primarily for tracking near-Earth asteroids. You might be surprised to learn that this telescope operates almost entirely remotely—our team controls it from a room downstairs, not from inside the dome itself. That's because the temperature inside the dome is kept very cold to reduce air turbulence, which can blur images.

Next, we'll move to the solar observation room, where we study sunspots and solar flares. Please note that you must not look directly at the sun through any of the equipment—it's extremely dangerous. Our staff will show you safe, projected images instead.

Finally, we'll end in the planetarium, where we'll present a short film about the life cycle of stars. The film lasts about 20 minutes, and afterwards you'll have a chance to ask questions.

One more thing: the observatory is a working research facility, so we ask you to stay with the group at all times and not touch any instruments. Photography is allowed, but please turn off your flash. Now, let's begin the tour.

title: City Museum Audio Guide
passage: Hello, and welcome to the City Museum. I'm your audio guide for today, and I'll be leading you through our most popular exhibits. Before we begin, a few practical points. The museum is open until 6 p.m., but the last entry to the special exhibition is at 4:30. So if you want to see the dinosaur skeletons, please head there first. Photography is allowed everywhere except in the Hall of Minerals, where flash can damage the light-sensitive crystals. Now, let's start with the main hall. On your left, you'll see a large mural showing the city as it looked in 1850. Notice the river, which was much wider then. As we move forward, we'll pass the ancient pottery collection. These bowls and jars were found just ten miles from here, during the construction of a new shopping center. The museum acquired them in 2018. If you look closely at the patterns, you can see they were made by hand, not on a wheel. Next, we'll enter the Hall of Minerals. Please keep your voices down, as the acoustics here are quite sensitive. After that, we'll visit the textile room, where you can try on a replica of a 19th-century coat. Finally, we'll end at the gift shop, which offers books and postcards. Any questions? Just ask a staff member in a blue vest.

title: Bramley Country Park
passage: Welcome to Bramley Country Park. I'm Sarah, the park ranger, and I'll give you a quick overview before you set off. The park covers 120 hectares of woodland and meadow, and it's been open to the public since 1987. The main entrance is where you're standing now, but there's a second gate near the lake that closes at 4 p.m., so if you're planning a late walk, come back through the main gate. The visitor centre is open daily from 9 to 5, except Mondays when it's closed for maintenance. Inside, you'll find a small café and a gift shop. Now, a few things to note: cycling is allowed only on the designated cycle track, which runs along the eastern edge of the park. Dogs are welcome but must be kept on a lead near the lake area, as there are nesting birds there in spring. Barbecues are strictly prohibited, but you can use the picnic tables near the playground. Finally, the woodland trail takes about 90 minutes at a leisurely pace, and I'd recommend sturdy shoes, as it can get muddy after rain. Enjoy your visit!

title: University Campus Tour
passage: Hello everyone, and welcome to the University of Riverton. I'm your guide, Sarah, and I'll be showing you around our beautiful campus today. Before we start, let me give you a quick overview of the layout. We're currently standing in front of the Main Library, which is the largest building on campus. To your left, you'll see the Student Union, where you can find cafeterias, a bookstore, and various student clubs. If you walk straight ahead past the library, you'll reach the Science Complex, which includes the biology, chemistry, and physics departments. Now, one important thing to note: the campus is divided into two main areas—the academic zone and the residential zone. The academic zone, where we are now, is on the north side, while the residential halls are on the south side, across the river. There's a footbridge connecting the two, but it's quite a walk—about 15 minutes. So if you're staying in the dorms, you might want to allow extra time to get to classes. Also, the campus shuttle runs every 20 minutes from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m., and it's free for students. Oh, and before I forget, the tour will last about 90 minutes, and we'll end at the cafeteria in the Student Union, where you can enjoy a complimentary coffee. Any questions so far?

title: Visit to the City Botanic Gardens
passage:
Hello everyone, and welcome to the City Botanic Gardens. I'm your guide for today, and I'm delighted to show you around. Before we set off, let me give you a quick overview of what you'll see and some practical tips.

The gardens were established in 1852 and cover about 20 hectares. They're home to over 5,000 species of plants from around the world. One of the highlights is the tropical glasshouse, which houses rare orchids and carnivorous plants. We'll spend about 30 minutes there.

Next, we'll walk along the riverbank path, where you can see our famous weeping willows. These trees were planted over a century ago and are a popular spot for photos. After that, we'll visit the rose garden, which is at its best in spring. Unfortunately, the fernery is closed for renovation until next month, so we'll skip that today.

A few reminders: please don't touch the plants, and stay on the paths. You're welcome to take photos, but no flash in the glasshouse. Also, the café near the entrance offers a 10% discount for tour groups, so keep your ticket. We'll finish at the gift shop in about two hours. Any questions?

title: Sleep and Health Talk
passage:
Good evening everyone. Thanks for coming to tonight's talk on sleep and health. I'm Dr. Helen Marsh, a sleep researcher at the city university. I'm here to share some surprising facts about sleep and give you practical tips.

First, let me ask: how many of you get less than seven hours of sleep? Quite a few hands. Well, you're not alone. Recent studies show that nearly 40 percent of adults sleep less than seven hours a night. But here's the thing: sleep isn't just rest. It's when your brain cleans itself, storing memories and removing toxins. Lack of sleep can lead to weight gain, weakened immunity, and even heart problems.

Now, a common myth is that you can catch up on sleep during the weekend. Actually, research suggests that weekend recovery sleep doesn't fully reverse the damage. Your body clock gets confused, making Monday mornings even harder.

So what can you do? Keep a regular schedule. Try to go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, even on weekends. Also, avoid screens an hour before bed—blue light tricks your brain into thinking it's daytime. And keep your bedroom cool, dark, and quiet. If you can't fall asleep after 20 minutes, get up and do something relaxing, like reading a book. Don't lie there worrying.

Next week, I'll talk about diet and sleep. Now, any questions?

If you're interested in accommodation, there's a housing Q&A at 12:30 in the dining hall — that's usually very popular, so arrive early to get a seat.

One more thing: lunch vouchers are available from the registration desk, but you need to collect them before 1 p.m. The cafeteria closes at 2, so don't leave it too late. Oh, and if you're thinking about applying, remember the early deadline for international students is January 15th — that's earlier than for UK applicants.

Right, let's begin. Please follow me.

title: Forestry Training Program Orientation
passage: Welcome to the Forestry Training Program orientation. I'm Rachel Kim, your coordinator. This six-week program is designed for people who want to work as forest technicians. title: The Rise of the Textile Industry in Manchester
passage: Welcome to the Manchester Heritage Walking Tour. I'm your guide, and today we'll explore how this city became the world's first industrial city. In the late 18th century, Manchester was a small market town. But everything changed with the invention of the spinning jenny and the water frame. These machines allowed cotton to be spun into thread much faster than by hand. The city's damp climate was actually perfect for spinning cotton, as the moisture prevented the threads from breaking. By 1830, over a hundred mills lined the banks of the River Irwell. Workers flocked from rural areas, and the population exploded from 25,000 to over 300,000 in just a few decades. However, conditions in the mills were harsh. Children as young as six worked twelve-hour shifts. The air was thick with cotton dust, leading to a lung disease called byssinosis. Despite these hardships, Manchester's textiles were exported worldwide, earning the nickname 'Cottonopolis'. Today, the red-brick mills have been converted into apartments, offices, and museums. As we walk along the canal, notice the surviving warehouses – they are a reminder of this remarkable industrial past.

title: Zoo Tour Orientation
passage:
Welcome to Greenfield Wildlife Park. I'm your guide, Mark, and I'll be giving you a brief orientation before you explore the park on your own. The park is divided into three main zones: the African Savanna, the Asian Rainforest, and the Australian Outback. The African Savanna is home to our lions, giraffes, and zebras. The giraffe feeding station is a popular spot, but please note that feeding times are at 11:30 AM and 2:30 PM only. 

Over in the Asian Rainforest, you'll find our two red pandas, which are part of a conservation breeding program. They're most active in the early morning, so if you want to see them moving around, head there first. The Australian Outback features kangaroos and emus, and there's a walk-through aviary where you can get up close to colorful parrots. 

A few practical tips: the park shuttle runs every 15 minutes, and the last one leaves at 4:45 PM. Also, please don't bring any outside food into the animal enclosures. If you get hungry, the Lakeside Café near the entrance serves snacks and drinks until 5 PM. Finally, keep an eye out for our volunteers in blue shirts—they're happy to answer any questions. Enjoy your visit!

title: Annual Charity Fun Run: Participant Briefing
passage:
Good morning everyone, and welcome to the briefing for this year's Annual Charity Fun Run, organized by the Riverside Community Trust. I'm Emma, your event coordinator. Let me quickly run through the key details so you're all set for Sunday.

First, registration opens at 8 a.m. at the main pavilion in Greenfield Park. Please bring your confirmation email and a photo ID. The run itself kicks off at 9:30 sharp — we're starting earlier than last year to avoid the midday heat.

There are two routes: a 5-kilometer family route, which is mostly flat and suitable for prams and wheelchairs, and a 10-kilometer challenge route that includes a steep section through the woods. Both start and finish at the same spot.

Water stations are located every 2.5 kilometers along both routes. We also have first-aid tents at the 3-kilometer and 7-kilometer marks. If you feel unwell at any point, please stop and alert a marshal — they're the volunteers in bright orange vests.

Now, a couple of practical points. Parking is very limited near the park, so we strongly recommend using the free shuttle bus from Riverside Station, which runs every 15 minutes from 7 a.m. Also, please note that dogs are not allowed on the course for safety reasons, though they're welcome in the spectator area near the finish line.

Finally, don't forget the post-run picnic at 11:30. All proceeds from food sales go to the Children's Hospital Fund. Any questions so far?

title: Library Reading Group Announcement
passage:
Hello everyone, and welcome to this month's update from the Riverside Library. I'm Emma, the reading group coordinator, and I have some important news about our book club.

First, the good news: our reading group has grown so much that we're moving to a larger room. Starting next month, we'll meet in the Community Hall on the second floor instead of the small meeting room near the entrance. The Community Hall is much bigger and has better lighting, so it should be more comfortable for everyone.

Now, about the books. For October, we've chosen 'The Silent Patient' by Alex Michaelides. It's a psychological thriller, quite different from last month's historical novel. We thought it would be a nice change of pace. The book is about 350 pages, so you have plenty of time to read it before our meeting on October 15th.

One more thing: we're starting a new system for borrowing books. Instead of buying your own copy, you can now borrow one from the library's book club collection. Just come to the front desk and ask for the reading group shelf. We have ten copies available, so it's first come, first served.

Finally, don't forget that our meeting time has changed slightly. We used to meet at 6:30, but now we'll start at 7:00 and finish at 8:30. That gives everyone a bit more time to get here after work.

If you have any questions, please email me or stop by the front desk. Happy reading!
