title: Office Hours Discussion on a Research Paper
passage: Professor: Hi, come in. What can I do for you? Student: Hi, Professor. I'm working on my research paper about urban green spaces, and I'm having trouble narrowing down my topic. I have too many ideas. Professor: That's a common issue. Let's start with your research question. What exactly do you want to find out? Student: Well, I'm interested in how green spaces affect mental health, but also how they impact property values and community engagement. Professor: That's quite broad. For a 10-page paper, you need to focus on one aspect. Which one interests you most? Student: Probably mental health. I found some studies linking access to parks with reduced stress. Professor: Good. So your research question could be: How does access to urban green spaces correlate with stress levels in different socioeconomic neighborhoods? Student: That sounds manageable. But I'm worried about data. Where can I find statistics on stress levels by neighborhood? Professor: You can use the city's public health database. Also, the university library has a subscription to a journal that publishes such studies. I can email you the details. Student: Thanks! That would really help. Should I also look at qualitative data, like interviews? Professor: For a short paper, stick to quantitative data. You can mention qualitative as a direction for future research. Student: Okay. So I'll focus on quantitative data from public health records and maybe a survey. Professor: Exactly. And remember to define your terms clearly—what do you mean by 'access'? Distance? Number of parks? Student: Good point. I'll define it as number of parks within a one-mile radius. Professor: Perfect. Now you have a clear plan.

title: Discussion about a Literature Review Assignment
passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Lee. Do you have a minute? I'm a bit confused about the literature review assignment for your Victorian Literature seminar.
Professor: Of course, come in. What's troubling you?
Student: Well, I've gathered a lot of sources on Dickens and social reform, but I'm not sure how to organize them. Should I just summarize each article one by one?
Professor: No, that would be too superficial. A literature review should synthesize the sources, not just list them. You need to identify key themes, debates, and gaps in the research. For example, you could group your sources by their arguments about Dickens's portrayal of poverty.
Student: I see. So I should show how the sources relate to each other?
Professor: Exactly. Also, make sure to evaluate the credibility of each source. Are they from peer-reviewed journals? Are the authors experts in the field?
Student: Okay. And how many sources do I need?
Professor: At least ten, but quality matters more than quantity. You can include a few primary sources, like reviews from the 19th century, but focus on recent scholarly articles.
Student: Got it. Thanks, Professor Lee. I feel much clearer now.
Professor: You're welcome. And remember, the draft is due next Friday. If you have more questions, come to my office hours.

title: Visa Renewal Woes
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between an international student and a university advisor.

Student: Hi, I'm here because I'm really worried about my visa renewal. My student visa expires next month, and I've already sent in my application, but I haven't heard anything back yet. I'm supposed to travel home for my sister's wedding in three weeks, and I'm afraid I won't be able to get back into the country.

Advisor: I understand your concern. Have you received a receipt notice from USCIS?

Student: Yes, I got a receipt notice about two weeks ago. It says they received my application, but it doesn't say anything about the processing time.

Advisor: OK, that's a good start. Normally, if you have a pending application and your current visa is still valid, you can travel, but you need to carry the receipt notice and other documents. However, if your visa expires while you're abroad, you won't be able to re-enter on that same visa. You'll need to get a new visa stamp at a U.S. consulate before coming back.

Student: That's the problem. I've heard that getting a new visa stamp can take weeks, and appointments are hard to get. My sister's wedding is in three weeks, and I really don't want to miss it.

Advisor: I see. One option is to wait until you receive your new I-20 and then travel with the receipt notice and the new I-20. But you should also check with the international office to see if they recommend traveling while your application is pending. Sometimes it's risky because if your application is denied while you're away, you might not be able to return.

Student: So what should I do?

Advisor: I'd suggest you make an appointment with our international student advisor to discuss your specific case. They can give you the most up-to-date advice. In the meantime, don't book any non-refundable tickets.

title: Library Research Help for a Paper on the 1918 Flu Pandemic
passage: Student: Hi, I’m working on a paper for my history class about the 1918 flu pandemic, and I’m having trouble finding enough sources. I need at least ten scholarly articles and a few primary sources. Could you help me? Librarian: Absolutely. So you’re looking for both secondary and primary sources. Let’s start with the databases. Have you tried JSTOR or PubMed? Student: I tried JSTOR, but most of the results were too broad—like global overviews. I need something more specific, maybe about how the pandemic affected a particular city or region. Librarian: Got it. You can narrow your search by adding keywords like “Philadelphia” or “New York City” and “1918 influenza.” Also, check the subject terms. That often leads to more focused articles. Student: That makes sense. What about primary sources? I’m not sure where to find letters or newspaper articles from that time. Librarian: For primary sources, try the library’s digital collections. We have a database called “Historical Newspapers” that includes archives from major papers. You can also look at the Internet Archive for digitized letters and diaries. Student: Oh, I didn’t know about those. One more thing—my professor said we should cite sources in Chicago style. Do you have a guide for that? Librarian: Yes, we have a citation guide on the library website, and you can also use the Chicago Manual of Style online. I’ll email you the links. Student: That would be great. Thanks so much! Librarian: No problem. If you need more help, just book a research consultation with me.

title: Credit Transfer Troubles
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a university admissions officer.

Student: Hi, I'm transferring from another university, and I was told I need to get my credits evaluated. Can you help me with that?

Officer: Of course. I'll need your official transcripts from your previous school. Have you brought them?

Student: Yes, here they are. I'm just worried because I took a lot of courses that might not match exactly with your curriculum.

Officer: Let me take a look. Hmm, you've taken Introduction to Statistics, but our equivalent is Quantitative Methods. That should transfer, but it might count as an elective, not a core requirement.

Student: Oh, that's a problem. I need it as a core for my major. Is there any way to appeal?

Officer: You can submit a syllabus and a course description to the department. They'll review it. But it might take a couple of weeks.

Student: I see. Also, I took a literature course that was about American poetry. Does that count for the humanities requirement?

Officer: It could, but our humanities requirement specifically requires a course with a writing-intensive component. Did your course have that?

Student: I'm not sure. I'll check the syllabus.

Officer: Good. Once you gather all the documents, bring them to me, and I'll forward them to the relevant departments. Just a heads-up: the deadline for transfer credit appeals is next Friday.

Student: Next Friday? That's soon. I'll get everything together as soon as possible. Thanks for your help.

Officer: You're welcome. And don't forget to fill out the transfer credit form online first.

Student: Okay, I'll do that right away.

title: Discussion with Teaching Assistant About a Lab Report
passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Lee? I'm sorry to bother you. I'm a bit confused about the lab report assignment for Biology 101.
Professor: No problem, come in. What's your question?
Student: Well, I've collected all my data from the experiment, but I'm not sure how to structure the report. The guidelines mention a 'Results' section and a 'Discussion' section, but I'm not clear on the difference.
Professor: That's a common confusion. The Results section is where you present your data—tables, graphs, observations—without any interpretation. Just the facts. The Discussion section is where you explain what those results mean. You interpret the data, relate it to your hypothesis, and discuss any errors or limitations.
Student: So I shouldn't include any analysis in the Results?
Professor: Exactly. Save all the analysis for the Discussion. Also, make sure you cite your sources properly. Last semester, several students lost points for improper citations.
Student: Got it. And how long should the report be?
Professor: There's no strict page limit, but aim for about 5 to 7 pages, double-spaced. The key is clarity and completeness, not length.
Student: Thanks, Professor. That helps a lot.
Professor: You're welcome. If you have more questions, feel free to email me or come to office hours.

choices.label: A
choices.text: To ask for an extension on a deadline

choices.label: B
choices.text: To clarify the structure of a lab report

choices.label: C
choices.text: To complain about a grade

choices.label: D
choices.text: To request a recommendation letter

questions.explanation: 考点：主旨。学生一开始就说对实验报告的结构感到困惑，之后的问题都围绕如何区分Results和Discussion部分。A、C、D在对话中均未提及。

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: A list of references

title: Library Research Help
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a librarian.

Student: Hi, excuse me. I'm working on a paper about the history of public transportation in the 19th century, and I'm having trouble finding primary sources. Could you help me?

Librarian: Of course. Let's start with the library catalog. What exactly are you looking for?

Student: Well, I need newspaper articles, maybe some city council records, and ideally, personal letters or diaries from that era. The problem is, I keep finding secondary sources—books that talk about the topic but don't have original documents.

Librarian: I see. Have you tried our special collections department? They have a lot of digitized archives—newspapers like The New York Times and The Times of London from the 1800s. Also, we subscribe to a database called 'American Periodicals' that includes magazines and journals from 1740 to 1940.

Student: Oh, I didn't know about that. I've only been searching the main catalog. How do I access the special collections?

Librarian: You need to make an appointment. They're open Monday to Friday, 10 to 4. But before you go, let me show you how to filter your search to primary sources only. Just use the 'archival materials' option in the advanced search.

Student: That's really helpful. Thanks so much!

Librarian: No problem. If you need more help, just come back. Good luck with your paper.

title: Scholarship Application Help
passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Martinez. Do you have a minute?
Professor: Of course, come in. What's on your mind?
Student: I'm applying for the Summer Research Grant, and I need a recommendation letter from a faculty member. I was hoping you could write one for me.
Professor: I'd be happy to. But the deadline is next Friday, right? That's a bit tight.
Student: Actually, the deadline is this Friday. I know it's short notice. I only found out yesterday that my previous recommender is on sabbatical and can't be reached.
Professor: I see. Well, I can do it, but I'll need your CV, your research proposal, and a copy of your transcript. Can you get those to me by tomorrow morning?
Student: Yes, absolutely. I'll email them tonight. Thank you so much.
Professor: One more thing—the grant committee also requires a personal statement. Have you written that yet?
Student: I've started it, but I'm not sure if it's specific enough. Could you take a quick look at it after I send it?
Professor: Sure, I can give you feedback, but don't wait for my comments to submit the letter request. The system closes at 5 p.m. on Friday.
Student: Got it. I'll send everything tonight and submit the request first thing tomorrow.
Professor: Perfect. And good luck—this grant is competitive, but your project on urban gardening sounds promising.

title: Inquiring About an Internship Opportunity
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a career advisor.

Student: Hi, Professor Adams. Thanks for meeting with me. I'm a junior in environmental science, and I'm hoping to get some advice on finding an internship for this summer. I've been looking at a few positions, but I'm not sure where to start.

Advisor: Of course, happy to help. Have you checked the university's online internship portal? That's usually the best first step. Many organizations post positions there specifically for our students.

Student: Yeah, I've browsed it a bit. But honestly, a lot of them require previous experience, which I don't have. I did volunteer at a local park last year, but that was mostly trail maintenance.

Advisor: That's actually more relevant than you think. Environmental consulting firms value hands-on fieldwork. You could highlight that in your application. Also, have you considered applying to the state environmental agency? They have a summer program for undergraduates with no prior internship experience.

Student: Oh, I didn't know that. Do they pay?

Advisor: Some positions are paid, but many are unpaid. However, you can often get academic credit through our department. You'd need to fill out a form and get approval from your faculty advisor.

Student: That sounds doable. When is the deadline for the state program?

Advisor: Let me check... The priority deadline is March 15th, but they accept applications until April 1st if spots remain. I'd recommend submitting by mid-March to be safe.

Student: Great. I'll start working on my application this week. Thanks so much!

title: Exchange Program Application Inquiry
passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Martinez. Do you have a minute? I'm thinking about applying to the exchange program with the University of Melbourne next semester, and I need some advice.
Professor: Of course, come in. You're the second student today asking about that. The application deadline is next Friday, so you're cutting it close. Have you started the paperwork?
Student: I've filled out the main form, but I'm stuck on the course equivalency section. It asks which of our courses match theirs, and I don't want to pick the wrong ones.
Professor: Smart. That's where most students mess up. You need to get your choices approved by the department chair, not just your advisor. And for the Melbourne program specifically, they require at least two courses in your major to be pre-approved before you go.
Student: Oh, I didn't know that. I thought my advisor's signature was enough. Also, do I need to submit a language test score? I took the TOEFL last year but it's expired now.
Professor: Yes, unfortunately. Melbourne requires a valid score within two years. But since you're a native speaker, you can take an internal placement test instead—it's free and offered every Wednesday.
Student: That's a relief. One last thing: the program brochure mentions a mandatory orientation in July. Is that online or on campus?
Professor: It's on campus, but they record it for those who can't attend. Still, I'd recommend going in person—you'll meet your future classmates and get priority for housing.
Student: Great. I'll book the placement test right away. Thanks, Professor!

title: Writing Center Session on a Research Paper
passage:
Listen to a conversation between a student and a writing center tutor.

Student: Hi, I'm here about my research paper for Environmental Science. I'm really stuck on the introduction.
Tutor: Sure, pull up a chair. What's the issue?
Student: Well, I've got all this data on microplastics in freshwater lakes, but I don't know how to start. I just jump straight into the methods, and it feels abrupt.
Tutor: I see. A good introduction usually moves from general to specific. You could open with the widespread presence of plastics, then narrow to microplastics, and finally state your research question.
Student: That makes sense. But my professor said my thesis is too vague. She wrote 'need a clear argument, not just a topic.'
Tutor: Exactly. A thesis should be debatable. For example, instead of 'This paper examines microplastics in Lake Erie,' try 'Microplastic concentrations in Lake Erie exceed safety thresholds primarily due to urban runoff, requiring immediate mitigation.' See the difference?
Student: Oh, yes. So I need to take a position. I was also thinking of adding a paragraph about previous studies, but I'm not sure where.
Tutor: That's a literature review. It usually comes right after the introduction, before your own methods. It shows how your work fits in.
Student: Got it. And should I mention my results in the intro?
Tutor: No, save those for the results section. The intro should end with your thesis, then the literature review. 
Student: Thanks. I think I can fix this now.

choices.label: C

passage:

title: Transferring Credits to a New University
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and an academic advisor.

Student: Hi, I'm Emily. I'm transferring here from another university next semester, and I have a question about my credits. I took a lot of courses there, but I'm not sure how many will transfer.

Advisor: Welcome, Emily. So, you'll need to submit official transcripts from your previous school. Our registrar will evaluate each course. Generally, courses with a grade of C or better are eligible for transfer, but it also depends on whether the course content matches something we offer.

Student: I see. What about courses that don't match exactly? Like, I took a course called 'Environmental Ethics'—it was in the philosophy department. We don't have that exact title here.

Advisor: Sometimes we can accept it as an elective if it's a 100 or 200 level. But if it's a 300 level or above, it might need approval from the department. You can file a petition with the department chair. They'll review the syllabus.

Student: Okay. And is there a limit on how many credits can transfer?

Advisor: Yes, typically up to 60 credits from a two-year college, or 90 from a four-year institution. But you need to complete at least 30 credits here to earn a degree.

Student: That's good to know. One more thing—do my grades transfer too, or just the credits?

Advisor: Just the credits. Your GPA starts fresh here. So even if you got a C in a course, it won't affect your new GPA.

Student: That's a relief. Thanks for explaining!

Advisor: You're welcome. Make sure to submit your transcripts by the deadline, which is July 1st.

title: Discussion with Teaching Assistant about a Psychology Assignment
passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Chen. Do you have a minute? I'm a bit confused about the assignment you gave in Psychology 101 last week.
Professor: Of course, come in. You're the second student today asking about it. What's your question?
Student: Well, the prompt says we need to design an experiment to test memory in college students, but it also says we have to include a 'control condition.' I'm not sure what that means exactly.
Professor: Ah, that's a common confusion. A control condition is a group that doesn't receive the experimental treatment, so you can compare the results. For example, if you're testing whether caffeine improves memory, one group drinks coffee, and the control group drinks decaf. That way you can see if the caffeine made the difference.
Student: Oh, I see. So the control group is basically a baseline.
Professor: Exactly. Also, remember to keep everything else the same—same time of day, same test, same instructions. Otherwise, you won't know what caused the change.
Student: Got it. And how many participants do we need?
Professor: At least twenty per group. The more, the better, but twenty is the minimum for statistical validity.
Student: Okay, that makes sense. Thanks so much. I'll get started on it right away.
Professor: You're welcome. And if you have any more questions, just email me. Good luck!

Librarian: Those are often on the websites of organizations like the EPA or the WHO. We have a guide for that. Let me show you how to access our research guide on environmental policy. It lists key websites and databases. 

Student: Great, thanks. I'll try those. 

Librarian: One more thing: if you find an article that's not in our collection, you can request it through interlibrary loan. It's free and usually takes about a week.

title: Transfer Credit Evaluation
passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Martinez. Do you have a minute?
Professor: Of course. What's on your mind?
Student: I'm thinking about transferring to another university next semester, and I'm a bit confused about how my credits will transfer.
Professor: That's a common concern. Have you checked with the registrar's office?
Student: Yes, but they said it depends on the receiving institution. I'm worried that some of my courses here won't count toward my major there.
Professor: Well, each university has its own transfer credit policy. Typically, they evaluate course syllabi and compare them to their own offerings. If the content matches, you get credit. But sometimes they only accept courses with similar credit hours.
Student: So if my course is 3 credits but theirs is 4, it might not transfer?
Professor: Exactly. Or they might accept it as an elective, not as a major requirement. You should also check if they have articulation agreements with our university. Those make transfers smoother.
Student: Articulation agreements? What are those?
Professor: Formal partnerships where specific courses are pre-approved for transfer. The registrar's office should have a list of partner schools. I'd recommend making an appointment with a transfer advisor there.
Student: I'll do that. Thanks for the advice, Professor.
Professor: My pleasure. Good luck!

title: Meeting with TA About Research Paper
passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Martinez? I'm sorry to bother you during office hours, but I'm really stuck on the research paper for your sociology class. I've been trying to narrow down my topic for weeks, but everything I come up with feels too broad or too narrow.
Professor: No problem at all, that's what office hours are for. Let's see if we can't figure this out. What was your original idea?
Student: Well, I wanted to write about how social media affects teenagers' mental health. But then I read a few articles and realized there's just so much out there. I don't know how to make it manageable.
Professor: That's actually a very common issue. The key is to find a specific angle. For example, instead of looking at all social media, you could focus on one platform, like Instagram, and one specific age group, say 13 to 15 year olds. And maybe explore how their self-esteem is impacted by 'likes'.
Student: That makes sense. So I should pick a narrower slice. But will I have enough sources? I need at least ten peer-reviewed articles.
Professor: Usually, the narrower you go, the easier it is to find focused studies. You might need to use a database like PsycINFO. And don't forget, you can also use the references from those articles to find more.
Student: Okay, that's helpful. Should I run my new topic by you before I start writing?
Professor: Absolutely. Send me a one-paragraph proposal by Friday, and I'll give you feedback.
Student: Great, thank you so much! I feel much better now.

title: Office Hours Discussion About a Research Paper
passage:
Professor: Hi, come in. You wanted to talk about your research paper?
Student: Yes, Professor. I'm a bit confused about the methodology section. I'm analyzing the effects of social media on teenage sleep patterns, and I've collected survey data from 200 high school students. But I'm not sure if I should also conduct interviews.
Professor: That depends on your research question. If you want to understand the 'why' behind the numbers, interviews would add depth. But they take time. You have three weeks left.
Student: I was thinking of interviewing about 20 students. Would that be enough?
Professor: For a qualitative component, 15 to 20 is reasonable. But you need to be careful about your sampling. Are you selecting from the same group who took the survey?
Student: Yes, I planned to randomly pick from those who volunteered.
Professor: Good. Also, remember to get parental consent for minors. That's crucial.
Student: Right, I almost forgot. I'll prepare the consent forms this week.
Professor: And one more thing: your literature review is a bit thin. You should include at least five more recent studies, especially those published after 2020.
Student: Okay, I'll look for more sources. Thank you, Professor.
Professor: You're welcome. Drop by next week if you have more questions.

title: Office Hours: Preparing for a Class Presentation
passage:
Professor: Come in, Alex. You wanted to talk about your presentation for Friday? 
Student: Yes, Professor. I'm a bit nervous. I've never given a presentation in front of the whole class before. I mean, I've done group projects, but this is solo. 
Professor: That's normal. How's your preparation going? 
Student: I think I have a good topic—the effects of social media on teenage sleep. I've got lots of statistics. But I'm not sure how to organize it. Should I start with the data or with a story? 
Professor: That depends. You want to grab their attention first. A short personal anecdote or a surprising fact works well. Then move to the data. But don't just read your slides. Make eye contact. 
Student: Okay. And how long should I talk? 
Professor: You have ten minutes, but aim for eight. Leave time for questions. Also, practice in front of a mirror or record yourself. 
Student: That's a good idea. I'll do that. Thanks, Professor. 
Professor: You're welcome. And remember, everyone gets nervous. Just breathe and focus on your message. 
Student: I'll try. See you Friday.

title: Discussion with Teaching Assistant About Assignment
passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Johnson. Do you have a minute? I'm a bit confused about the assignment you gave in class today.
Professor: Of course, come in. What's the issue?
Student: Well, you mentioned that we need to write a research paper on a topic related to environmental science, but I'm not sure how to narrow it down. The guidelines say it should be 8-10 pages, but I'm struggling to pick a specific angle.
Professor: That's a common concern. The key is to choose a topic that you're genuinely interested in, but also one that has enough scholarly sources. What areas of environmental science appeal to you?
Student: I'm interested in renewable energy, especially solar power. But I'm worried it might be too broad.
Professor: Good choice. You could focus on a specific aspect, like the efficiency of solar panels in urban areas, or the economic challenges of implementing solar energy in developing countries. That would give you a clear direction.
Student: That sounds helpful. Should I include case studies?
Professor: Absolutely. Case studies can strengthen your argument and provide concrete examples. Also, remember to use peer-reviewed sources. The library has a great database for that.
Student: Great. When is the deadline again?
Professor: The paper is due on the 15th of next month. But you need to submit an outline by the end of this week. I'll review it and give you feedback.
Student: Oh, I almost forgot about the outline. I'll get started right away. Thanks, Professor!
Professor: You're welcome. Good luck!

title: Writing Center Session
passage:
Hi, Professor, I'm here about my paper for American Literature. The assignment says we need to analyze a theme in a short story, but I'm not sure if my thesis is strong enough. I chose 'The Lottery' by Shirley Jackson and want to argue that the story criticizes blind tradition. Is that too obvious?

Actually, that's a common interpretation, but not necessarily too obvious. The key is how you support it. Have you looked at the specific language Jackson uses, like the casual dialogue before the stoning? That contrast could make your argument fresh.

I didn't focus on that. I mainly summarized the plot. My draft is due Friday, and I have a chemistry exam Thursday.

Okay, let's prioritize. You don't need to rewrite everything. Start by adding one paragraph analyzing the dialogue. Use two quotes. That should deepen your thesis. Also, check your conclusion. It currently just restates the introduction. Try connecting it to a modern example of ritualized violence.

That sounds doable. Should I come back after I revise?

Yes, but don't wait until Friday morning. My drop-in hours are Tuesday and Wednesday from 2 to 4. If you come Wednesday, you'll have time to make final changes. And bring your chemistry notes if you want—we can talk about time management, too.

Thanks, Professor. I'll see you Wednesday.

passage:
Student: Hi, Professor Lee. Do you have a minute? I'm a bit stuck on the research paper topic for your sociology class.

Professor: That's much better. You could examine the correlation between Instagram use and self-esteem in adolescent girls. But remember, you'll need empirical studies, not just opinions.
Student: I found a few articles in the library database, but they're mostly from 2015. Is that too old?
Professor: For a literature review, you should aim for sources from the last five years. Try searching with keywords like "body image" and "social comparison" to find recent studies. Also, check the reference lists of those older articles—they might lead you to newer work.
Student: Okay, I'll do that. Should I include a section on potential solutions, like media literacy programs?
Professor: That could be a good addition, but keep it brief. The main focus should be on the analysis. And don't forget to submit your outline by next Friday.

title: Office Hours: Planning a Class Presentation on Urban Farming
passage:
Narrator: Listen to a conversation between a student and a professor.

Student: Hi, Professor Martinez. Do you have a minute? I wanted to talk about my presentation for next week.

Professor: Of course, come in. You're presenting on urban agriculture, right?

Student: Yes. I've got a lot of information, but I'm not sure how to organize it. I was thinking of covering the history of community gardens, then vertical farming, then maybe some policy issues.

Professor: That's a lot for a ten-minute talk. You need to focus. What's your main argument?

Student: Well, I guess that urban farming can help food deserts—neighborhoods without easy access to fresh produce.

Professor: Good. So build everything around that. Start with the problem, then show two or three concrete examples of how urban farms address it. Keep the history and policy brief—maybe just as background.

Student: Should I use slides?

Professor: Yes, but keep them visual. A few photos and a simple chart, not paragraphs of text. And remember, you'll have about two minutes for questions, so be ready to explain your sources.

Student: Got it. I'll restructure my outline tonight.

Professor: Good. Send me a draft by Friday if you want feedback.

Man: It's Daniel Okafor. That's O-K-A-F-O-R.
Woman: Thank you, Mr Okafor. And the address?
Man: 42 Maple Crescent, Flat 3B. The postcode is BR5 2QT.
Woman: Got it. What's the make and model of the machine?
Man: It's a Zanussi, model ZX740. We bought it about three years ago.
Woman: And when would you like an engineer to visit?
Man: Well, I work during the day, so any time after 5 pm on weekdays would be best. Or Saturday morning.

Man: Thursday at 5:30 works perfectly.
Woman: Great. There's a standard call-out fee of £45, which covers the first hour. Parts are extra. Is that okay?
Man: Yes, that's fine.
Woman: Could I also get a mobile number in case the engineer is delayed?
Man: Sure, it's 07700 900348.
Woman: Perfect. We'll send you a text confirmation shortly. Anything else?
Man: No, that's all. Thanks very much.
Woman: You're welcome. Goodbye.

title: Joining the City Library
passage:
Librarian: Good morning. Welcome to the City Library. How can I help you today?
Student: Hi, I'd like to join the library. I'm new in town.
Librarian: Of course. Are you a student here?
Student: Yes, I'm doing a master's in environmental science at the university.
Librarian: Great. Can I see your student ID and proof of address?
Student: I have my student card, but I don't have a utility bill yet. I just moved into a flat last week.
Librarian: That's fine. A tenancy agreement or a bank statement with your address will work too.
Student: I have a bank statement here. Will that do?
Librarian: Perfect. Now, what kind of membership would you like? We have standard and premium. Standard is free for students, and you can borrow up to five books for two weeks. Premium costs twenty pounds a year and allows ten books for three weeks, plus free access to the online journal database.
Student: The premium sounds useful for my research, but I'm on a tight budget. Can I start with the standard and upgrade later?
Librarian: Absolutely. You can upgrade anytime. Just so you know, standard members can still use the computers and Wi-Fi, but you'll need to pay a small fee for printing.
Student: That's okay. I'll go with standard for now.
Librarian: Alright. Let me set that up for you. You'll get your card in a few minutes.

questions.question: Why is the student at the library?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To return some overdue books

choices.label: B
choices.text: To apply for a library membership

choices.label: C
choices.text: To ask about a research project

choices.label: D
choices.text: To pay a printing fee

questions.explanation: 考点：主旨。学生明确说“I'd like to join the library”，即申请图书馆会员。A项未提及；C项研究项目只是后续提到数据库时关联，非目的；D项打印费是标准会员的额外费用，非来访原因。

choices.label: B

questions.explanation: 考点：细节。学生说没有水电费账单，但提供了银行对账单（bank statement），图书管理员确认可以。A项学生没有；B项管理员提到可接受但学生未提供；D项学生证是身份证明，非地址证明。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the student's choice of membership?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The student chose premium for the online database.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The student will upgrade to premium immediately.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The student decided on standard due to cost concerns.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The student is not eligible for any free membership.

questions.explanation: 考点：推断。学生说“I'm on a tight budget”并选择先办标准会员，可推断经济因素是主要考虑。A项学生认为高级会员有用但未选；B项学生说以后可能升级；D项标准会员对 students 免费，故不成立。

title: Purchasing Insurance
passage:
Agent: Good morning, Lakeside Insurance. How can I help you?
Customer: Hi, I'd like to get a quote for home insurance. I'm moving into a new apartment next month.
Agent: Congratulations! I can help with that. Could you tell me the address?
Customer: It's 42 Maple Street, Apartment 3B.
Agent: Got it. Is it a rental or do you own it?
Customer: I'm renting. The landlord requires tenants to have contents insurance.
Agent: Understood. We offer two plans: Basic and Comprehensive. Basic covers fire, theft, and water damage up to $20,000. Comprehensive adds accidental damage and covers up to $50,000. Which would you prefer?
Customer: I think Comprehensive sounds better. How much is it per month?
Agent: For your area, Comprehensive is $35 per month, or $380 if you pay annually. Basic is $22 monthly.
Customer: I'll go with Comprehensive, paid monthly. Can I start the policy on the 15th?
Agent: Sure. I'll need your ID and proof of address. You can email them to us.
Customer: Great, I'll send them today. Thanks!

questions.question: Why does the customer contact the insurance company?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To file a claim for water damage

choices.label: B
choices.text: To get a quote for home insurance

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

questions.question: What is the monthly cost of the Comprehensive plan?
questions.explanation: 考点：细节题。代理明确说‘Comprehensive is $35 per month’，C正确。A项$20,000是保额；B项$22是Basic的月费；D项$380是年付价格。

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are a landlord looking for tenant insurance.

questions.explanation: 考点：推断题。客户说‘I'm renting. The landlord requires tenants to have contents insurance.’，可推断他们租房且需要财物保险，B正确。A项是业主；C项买房；D项是房东，均与原文矛盾。

title: IELTS Listening Section 1: Course Enrollment Conversation
passage:
Receptionist: Good morning, Riverside Community College. How can I help you?
Student: Hi, I'd like to enroll in a course. I saw the advertisement for the evening pottery class.
Receptionist: Certainly. The pottery class runs on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 6 to 8 p.m. It's a 10-week course starting on September 15th.
Student: That sounds good. How much does it cost?
Receptionist: The fee is $180, which includes all materials and a small exhibition at the end.
Student: Is there a discount for students?
Receptionist: Yes, if you bring your student ID, you get 15% off. So it would be $153.
Student: Great. Can I pay by card?
Receptionist: We accept card, cash, or bank transfer. But card payments have a $2 processing fee. Cash is fine, no extra charge.
Student: I'll pay in cash then. What do I need to bring on the first day?
Receptionist: Just an apron and an old towel. We provide the clay and tools. Also, please arrive 10 minutes early to fill out a form.
Student: OK. Do I need to register in advance?
Receptionist: Yes, we need your name and phone number. You can do it over the phone now if you like.
Student: Yes, please. My name is Sarah Jenkins, and my number is 07700 900123.
Receptionist: Got it. See you on the 15th.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the conversation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To enroll in a pottery course

choices.label: B
choices.text: To inquire about a job at the college

choices.label: C
choices.text: To complain about a course fee

choices.label: D
choices.text: To ask about a different evening class

questions.explanation: 考点：主旨理解。对话开头学生说‘I'd like to enroll in a course’并明确提到pottery class，之后一直在讨论报名细节，所以主旨是报名陶艺课。B未提及工作；C没有抱怨费用；D虽然提到其他晚上课程但并非主旨。

questions.question: How much will the student pay if she pays in cash?
questions.explanation: 考点：细节计算。原价$180，学生折扣15%，所以$180×0.85=$153。现金支付无额外费用，所以最终$153。A是原价；C是$153+$2（卡支付手续费）；D是错误计算。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the student's payment method?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She will pay by card because it is convenient.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She will pay by bank transfer to avoid fees.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She will pay in cash to avoid the extra charge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She will pay in cash because she doesn't have a card.

questions.explanation: 考点：推断。学生问‘Can I pay by card?’，接待员说卡支付有$2手续费，学生说‘I'll pay in cash then’，可推断她是为了避免额外费用。A相反；B未提及；D文中未说她没有卡。

title: Visa Application Phone Call
passage:
W: Good morning, City Travel Agency. How can I help you?
M: Hi, I'd like to ask about visa application for my trip to Spain. I'm planning to go in June.
W: Sure. First, what's the purpose of your visit—tourism or business?
M: Tourism. I'll be there for two weeks.
W: Then you'll need a Schengen visa. We can help you with the documents. You'll need a passport valid for at least three months after your return, a completed application form, two photos, travel insurance, and proof of accommodation.
M: I see. Do I need to show bank statements?
W: Yes, for the past three months. And a letter from your employer confirming your position and salary.
M: I'm self-employed. What should I do?
W: In that case, you need to provide your business registration and tax records for the last two years.
M: That sounds complicated. How long does the process take?
W: Normally about 15 working days, but in summer it can take up to 30 days. I'd advise you to apply at least six weeks before your departure.
M: OK. And what's the fee?
W: The embassy fee is 80 euros, and our service charge is 50 pounds. You can pay by card or bank transfer.
M: Alright. Can I book an appointment now?
W: Certainly. How about next Tuesday at 10 a.m.?
M: That works. Thank you.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the man's call?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To book a flight to Spain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To inquire about visa application requirements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To complain about a travel agency.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To apply for travel insurance.

questions.explanation: 主旨题。对话开头男士就说想询问去西班牙的签证申请（ask about visa application），之后所有内容都围绕签证材料、费用、时间等展开。A 是订机票，未提及；C 是投诉，无中生有；D 是申请旅行保险，虽然保险是签证材料之一，但不是打电话的主要目的。

questions.question: What additional document does the man need to provide because he is self-employed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A letter from his employer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bank statements for the past three months.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Business registration and tax records.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Proof of accommodation.

questions.explanation: 细节题。女士提到受雇者需要雇主信，但男士说自己是个体经营者（self-employed），女士随即说需要提供营业执照和过去两年的税务记录（business registration and tax records）。A 是受雇者所需，B 和 D 是所有人都需要的基本材料，不是因自雇而额外需要的。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the man's travel plans?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He will leave for Spain in less than a month.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He has already booked an appointment for next Tuesday.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He plans to stay in Spain for two weeks in June.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He will pay the fee by bank transfer.

questions.explanation: 推断题。男士明确说计划六月去，待两周（I'm planning to go in June... I'll be there for two weeks），因此 C 正确。A 错误，因为现在申请，六月出发，通常超过一个月；B 错误，他刚刚同意预约下周二，但还未最终确认（对话结尾只是说 That works，但预约尚未正式完成，且选项说已经预订，过于绝对）；D 错误，女士说可以刷卡或银行转账，男士尚未选择支付方式。

title: Pet Shop Inquiry
passage:
A: Good morning, welcome to Paws & Claws Pet Shop. How can I help you?
B: Hi, I'm thinking about getting a dog for my apartment. I've heard that some breeds are better suited for small spaces.
A: Absolutely. Do you have any experience with dogs?
B: Not really. This would be my first pet. I'm a bit worried about leaving it alone while I'm at work.
A: That's a common concern. For first-time owners in apartments, I'd suggest a breed that's low-energy and doesn't bark much. The French Bulldog is a good example. They're small, affectionate, and adapt well to indoor life.
B: That sounds promising. How much exercise do they need?
A: About 20 to 30 minutes of walking per day. They don't need a big yard. But they can have breathing problems, so you should avoid long walks in hot weather.
B: Good to know. What about grooming?
A: They shed a little, but a weekly brush is enough. And you'll need to clean their ears regularly.
B: Okay. And how much do they usually cost?
A: From a reputable breeder, around $1,500 to $2,500. But I'd also recommend checking rescue organizations—you might find one for a much lower adoption fee.
B: I'll look into that. Thanks for the advice.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the conversation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To buy pet supplies for an existing dog

choices.label: B
choices.text: To get advice on choosing a dog for an apartment

choices.label: C
choices.text: To complain about a pet shop's service

choices.label: D
choices.text: To apply for a job at a pet shop

questions.explanation: 考点：主旨理解。对话中男士明确表示想为公寓养一只狗，并询问品种建议，女士则给出推荐和注意事项。A 项“为已有的狗买用品”未提及；C 项“投诉”无中生有；D 项“求职”完全不符。因此选 B。

questions.question: According to the assistant, why is the French Bulldog suitable for the man?

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is inexpensive to buy.

questions.explanation: 考点：细节捕捉。女士提到 French Bulldog 是 low-energy and doesn't bark much，适合公寓和初次养狗者。A 项“不需要运动”与原文“每天散步 20-30 分钟”矛盾；B 项“容易训练”未提及；D 项“便宜”与原文价格 $1,500-$2,500 不符。因此选 C。

questions.question: What does the assistant imply about getting a French Bulldog from a breeder?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is the only way to get a healthy dog.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It may be more expensive than adopting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is not recommended for first-time owners.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It requires a waiting list of several months.

questions.explanation: 考点：推断理解。女士提到从 reputable breeder 购买需要 $1,500-$2,500，但建议查看 rescue organizations，因为 adoption fee 可能低得多。由此可推断 breeder 购买可能比领养更贵。A 项“唯一途径”过于绝对；C 项与女士推荐 French Bulldog 给初次养狗者矛盾；D 项“等待名单”未提及。因此选 B。

title: Courier Service Phone Inquiry
passage:
Woman: Good morning. I'd like to send a parcel to Edinburgh, please. Can you tell me about your services?
Man: Certainly. We offer standard delivery, which takes three to five working days, and express delivery, which is guaranteed next day by 1 pm. Which would you prefer?
Woman: I think standard is fine. It's not urgent. How much would it cost for a parcel weighing about two kilograms?
Man: Let me check. Standard delivery for up to two kilograms is £8.50. That includes tracking and a signature on delivery.
Woman: That sounds reasonable. Do I need to bring it to your office, or can you collect it?
Man: We can arrange a pickup, but there's an extra charge of £3. Alternatively, you can drop it off at any of our local shops. There's one on Mill Road, just next to the post office.
Woman: I'll drop it off, then. What do I need to do to prepare the parcel?
Man: Please make sure it's securely wrapped and clearly addressed. Also, don't include any fragile items without marking them. If you're sending liquids, they must be in leak-proof containers.
Woman: OK. And how long will it take to arrive?
Man: With standard delivery to Edinburgh, it usually takes three to four working days, but it can be up to five. You'll get a tracking number by email once it's scanned.

choices.label: A
choices.text: To ask about sending a parcel to Edinburgh

choices.label: C

questions.question: How much will the woman pay for standard delivery of her parcel?
questions.explanation: 考点：细节题。男士明确说“Standard delivery for up to two kilograms is £8.50.”。A 选项 £3 是上门取件的额外费用，C 选项是两者相加，D 选项未提及。

questions.question: What can be inferred about the woman's preference for dropping off the parcel?

choices.label: B
choices.text: She lives far from the courier's office.

choices.text: She needs the parcel to arrive urgently.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She prefers to pay extra for convenience.

questions.explanation: 考点：推断题。男士提到上门取件需额外支付 £3，女士随后说“I'll drop it off, then.”，可推断她选择自己送去是为了避免额外费用。B、C、D 均与对话内容不符。

title: Calling to Book a Dental Appointment
passage:
Receptionist: Good morning, Greenfield Dental Clinic. How can I help you?
Caller: Hi, I'd like to book an appointment with a dentist. I've been having some pain in my lower back tooth when I eat sweet things.
Receptionist: I see. Are you a registered patient with us?

Receptionist: That's fine. Can I take your full name and date of birth, please?

title: IELTS Exam Registration Phone Call
passage:
Woman: Good morning, City Language Centre. How can I help you?
Man: Hi, I'd like to register for the IELTS test, please. Could you tell me the available dates?
Woman: Of course. The next test is on Saturday, 15th March. We also have one on 5th April, but the March date is more popular, so it's filling up fast.
Man: I see. And what's the fee?
Woman: It's £195 if you register before the 1st of March. After that, the standard fee is £215. So I'd recommend booking early.

Man: Okay. Do I need to bring anything on the test day?

Man: Got it. Can I register online?

title: Hotel Room Booking Enquiry
passage:

W: I'm afraid the sea view room has a queen-size bed. But we can provide an extra blanket if needed.

W: Normally check-in is at 2 p.m., but I can note your request. It depends on housekeeping. We'll do our best.

title: Reporting a Faulty Washing Machine
passage:
Good morning, Citywide Appliance Repairs. How can I help you?

Oh, hello. I'm calling about my washing machine. It's been leaking water all over the kitchen floor.

I see. Can I take your name and address first, please?

Yes, it's Sarah Mitchell. That's M-I-T-C-H-E-L-L. And the address is 42 Greenfield Road, Flat 3B.

Thank you. And a contact number?

It's 07700 900348.

Great. Now, could you tell me the make and model of the machine?

It's a Bosch, I think. The model number is WAT28460GB.

And when did you first notice the problem?

About three days ago, but it's getting worse. Yesterday it flooded the whole floor.

Alright. Our engineer can come out on Thursday afternoon, between two and four. Would that work?

Thursday afternoon is fine. But could you ask the engineer to call me about half an hour before arriving? I need to leave work early.

Of course. Is there anything else?

Actually, yes. The machine is still under warranty, so I shouldn't have to pay, right?

If it's under two years old, the repair is free. Just have your receipt ready.

Perfect, thank you.

title: Booking a Flight to Sydney
passage:
Good morning, thank you for calling Global Air. My name is Sarah. How can I help you today?

Hi, I'd like to book a flight from London to Sydney, please.

Certainly. When would you like to travel?

I was thinking of leaving on the 15th of July, and returning on the 30th.

Let me check availability. Do you have a preferred time of day for departure?

Yes, I'd prefer an evening flight if possible, as I need to work during the day.

Alright. We have a flight departing at 7:30 PM, arriving in Sydney at 6:00 AM two days later. Is that suitable?

That sounds fine. How much would that cost?

Let me see... for economy class, the return ticket is £1,200. Would you like to book that?

Is there any baggage allowance included?

Yes, you can check in one suitcase up to 23 kilograms, and you can also take one carry-on bag.

Great. Can I pay by credit card?

Absolutely. Could I have your name and contact details, please?

Yes, it's John Smith. My phone number is 07700 900123.

Thank you, Mr. Smith. Your booking reference will be sent to you by email shortly.

title: Booking a Removal Company
passage:
Woman: Good morning. I'd like to get a quote for moving my furniture to a new flat next month.

Man: Certainly. Can I take your name and the moving date?

Woman: It's Sarah Mitchell. We're hoping to move on the 14th of July, a Saturday.

Man: Let me check... I'm afraid we're fully booked that weekend. The earliest we could do is Monday the 16th.

Woman: Oh, that's a problem. Our lease ends on the 15th. Could you do Friday the 13th instead?

Man: Friday the 13th is available. Now, how many bedrooms is the current place?

Woman: It's a two-bedroom flat, but we've got a lot of books and a piano.

Man: A piano will need special handling. That adds about 80 pounds. Our standard rate for a two-bedroom move is 450 pounds, including packing materials.

Woman: Does that cover insurance?

Man: Basic coverage up to 1,000 pounds is included. For full coverage, it's an extra 40 pounds. I'd strongly recommend it for the piano.

Woman: Alright, let's include that. What time will the team arrive?

Man: We usually start at 8 a.m., but we can do 9 if that suits you better.

Woman: 8 is fine. And could you send the confirmation by email? I'll pay the deposit online.

Man: No problem. I'll send it this afternoon.

title: Booking a Restaurant for an Anniversary Dinner
passage:
Woman: Good morning, thank you for calling The Olive Grove Restaurant. How can I help you?
Man: Hi, I'd like to book a table for this Saturday evening. It's for our wedding anniversary.
Woman: Lovely! How many people will be dining?

questions.question: What time will the man's table be reserved for?

title: IELTS Listening Section 1: Asking for Directions to the Train Station

Woman: Okay, I'll back it up. One more thing—do you use original parts?

title: Riverside Park Information Session
passage:
Hello everyone, and welcome to Riverside Park. I'm Sarah, your guide for today. Before we start our walk, let me give you a quick overview of the park and its facilities. Riverside Park covers 120 acres along the riverbank. It was established in 1920 and originally served as a private estate. The city purchased it in 1975 and opened it to the public.

The park has three main areas: the Rose Garden, the Wetlands, and the Adventure Playground. The Rose Garden is home to over 200 varieties of roses and is particularly beautiful in early summer. The Wetlands are a protected habitat for several bird species, so please stay on the marked paths. The Adventure Playground is designed for children aged 5 to 12 and includes a zip line and climbing wall.

Facilities include a café near the main entrance, open daily from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., and public restrooms next to the playground. Bicycle rentals are available at the boathouse on weekends. Please note that dogs must be kept on a leash at all times. Also, we kindly ask you not to feed the ducks, as it can harm their health. 

Now, if you have any questions, feel free to ask. Let's begin our tour.

That's where you'll find the cafeteria, the game room, and the offices for all the clubs. If you're interested in joining a club, just drop by the student union desk and they'll help you sign up. title: Bristol Harbourside Walking Tour
passage:
Hello everyone, and welcome to Bristol. I'm your guide, Mark, and today we'll explore the Harbourside, a area that has changed a lot over the past thirty years. As we walk, please stay on the left side of the path—the right side is for cyclists, and they can come up quite fast. Our tour lasts about ninety minutes, and we'll finish at the M Shed museum, where you can get a free map and use the toilets.

Our first stop is the SS Great Britain, just five minutes from here. That ship was designed by Isambard Kingdom Brunel and was the first iron steamship to cross the Atlantic. If you'd like to go inside after the tour, tickets are usually fourteen pounds, but I can give you a discount code for ten percent off.

Next, we'll pass the Watershed, a media centre with a nice café. Then we'll cross Pero's Bridge—locals call it the Horned Bridge because of its two horn-like sculptures. After that, we'll visit the Georgian House, a preserved merchant's home from the 1790s. It's free to enter, but donations are welcome.

Finally, a word of warning: the cobblestones near the harbour can be slippery when wet, so please watch your step. And if you need to take photos, step to the side so others can pass. Any questions before we start?

title: Volunteer Recruitment at Riverside Park
passage:
Hello everyone, and thanks for coming to this information session about volunteering at Riverside Park. I’m Emma, the volunteer coordinator here. We’re really excited to have so many new faces today.

Let me start with a bit of background. Riverside Park has been running for over thirty years, but in the last five years, visitor numbers have doubled. That’s great news, but it also means we need more help than ever to keep the park clean, safe, and welcoming.

We have three main volunteer roles. First, there are the garden assistants. They help plant and water flowers, and they also remove weeds. No experience is necessary—we’ll train you. Second, we have visitor guides. These volunteers lead short tours on weekends and answer questions at the information desk. You need to be comfortable speaking to groups. Third, we need event helpers. They assist with our seasonal festivals, like the summer concert and the autumn fair. That role is more flexible—you can sign up for just one event if you like.

All volunteers must attend a one-hour training session. We run these every Tuesday at 4 p.m. and Saturday at 10 a.m. You can choose whichever suits you. Also, you need to be at least sixteen years old. If you’re under eighteen, you’ll need a parent or guardian to sign a consent form.

Finally, a few practical points. We provide gloves, tools, and a free T-shirt. But please bring your own water bottle and wear comfortable shoes. And if you’re interested, please fill out the sign-up sheet at the back of the room before you leave. Any questions?

title: City Art Museum's New Exhibition: The Art of Repair
passage:
Welcome to the City Art Museum. I'm your guide for today's exhibition, 'The Art of Repair', which opens tomorrow and runs until the end of next month. This exhibition is a bit different—it focuses on how artists have turned broken or discarded objects into works of art. You'll see sculptures made from old bicycle parts, ceramics repaired with gold, and even a dress woven from plastic bags found on beaches. The idea is to challenge our throwaway culture and show that damage can add value, not reduce it. 

Now, a few practical points. The exhibition is on the second floor, in the west wing. Please note that the main lift is currently out of order, so you'll need to use the stairs or the smaller lift near the café. Photography is allowed, but no flash, as some artworks are light-sensitive. There's a free guided tour at 2 p.m. daily, but you need to sign up at the information desk. Also, the museum shop has a special range of recycled gifts, and all profits go to environmental charities. Finally, don't miss the interactive room where you can try your hand at repairing a broken pot using the Japanese art of kintsugi. It's great fun for all ages.

title: Riverside Fitness Centre Orientation Talk

title: Evening Course in Emergency First Aid at Work
passage:
Good evening, everyone, and thanks for coming out on such a wet night. My name's Karen Patel, and I coordinate the short courses at Bridgeford Community College. Tonight I want to tell you about our new evening course in Emergency First Aid at Work, which starts on the fourteenth of March.

Let me begin with the practical details. The course runs for six weeks, every Tuesday from six thirty to eight thirty, so it's designed for people who are already working full-time. You don't need any previous medical knowledge — about half of last year's group had never done any first aid training at all. The only thing you do need is to be at least sixteen years old. The fee is one hundred and twenty pounds, but if your employer agrees to send you, they can usually claim part of that back through a government training scheme.

Now, a word about the assessment, because this is where people often get confused. There's no written exam. Instead, you'll be assessed on your practical skills during the final session — things like bandaging, and what to do if someone stops breathing. You'll get a certificate at the end, and it's valid for three years. After that, you'd need to take a short refresher course to keep it up to date.

One last thing — please don't leave booking too late. We only have twenty places, and last term the course was full three weeks before it began. You can sign up online or at the front desk.

title: Welcome to the City Science Museum
passage:
Hello everyone, and welcome to the City Science Museum. I'm Sarah, your guide for today. Before we start, let me give you a quick overview. The museum is divided into three main sections: the Discovery Hall, the Innovation Zone, and the Future Lab. 

The Discovery Hall is on the ground floor, just behind me. There you'll find interactive exhibits about physics and biology. It's great for kids, but adults love it too. 

On the first floor, you'll find the Innovation Zone. This area focuses on engineering and technology. You can try building your own bridge or design a simple robot. Just a heads-up: the robot design activity is very popular, so you might need to wait in line. 

The Future Lab is on the second floor. It's a bit different — it's a quiet space where you can explore virtual reality and artificial intelligence. Please note that the Future Lab closes at 4:30 PM, half an hour earlier than the rest of the museum. 

Also, don't miss the live science show at 2 PM in the theater next to the café. It's about 30 minutes long and it's free with your ticket. 

If you have any questions, feel free to ask me. Enjoy your visit!

passage: Hello everyone, this is a message for all students and parents about our annual school sports day, which will take place next Friday, the 15th of June. Buses will leave from the school main gate at 8:30 a.m. sharp, so please arrive by 8:15. The first event, the 100-meter sprint, starts at 9:30. title: The Riverside Film Festival Schedule
passage: Welcome, everyone, to this short talk about the Riverside Film Festival, which runs from the twelfth to the eighteenth of July. I'm the festival coordinator, and I'd like to give you a quick overview of this year's programme. First, a few practical points. All screenings take place at the Old Mill Cinema on Dock Street, not at the Riverside Theatre as in previous years, because that building is being renovated. Tickets are eight pounds for adults and five for students, but if you buy a full-week pass for thirty pounds, you can attend as many films as you like. Now, let me highlight three events. On the opening night, we're showing a restored print of a 1950s Italian comedy, with a short introduction by the film historian Dr. Eleanor Vance. On Saturday afternoon, there's a documentary about deep-sea exploration, followed by a question-and-answer session with the director. And on the final evening, we're screening the winner of our short-film competition, chosen from over two hundred entries. One more thing: the festival café will be open until midnight each day, serving light meals and drinks. Booking is strongly recommended, especially for the weekend events, as seating is limited. You can book online or by phone, but please note that phone bookings close at five p.m. on the day before each screening. I'll now take a few questions.

title: City Library Makerspace Workshop Announcement
passage:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the monthly orientation for the City Library Makerspace. I'm Daniel, the program coordinator, and I'll be walking you through our upcoming weekend workshops. First, a quick note: registration for all workshops opens this Friday at 9 a.m. online, not in person as in previous seasons. We've had huge demand, so please set a reminder. 

Our most popular session is the beginner's pottery wheel class. It runs Saturday from 1 to 4 p.m. and costs fifteen dollars, which covers clay, tools, and firing. Because space is limited to eight people, we ask that you cancel at least 48 hours in advance if you can't attend, so someone on the waiting list can take your spot. Last month, three people simply didn't show up, and that was a real shame. 

The second workshop is hand-built ceramics, where you shape clay without a wheel. That one is free for library members, five dollars for non-members, and it's on Sunday morning at 10. 

Finally, a new addition: a two-hour leather tooling workshop on Saturday evening. It's aimed at adults, though ages 14 and up are welcome with a guardian. The instructor, Maria, has over twenty years of experience, and she'll teach you to stamp, carve, and dye a small wallet. 

Please note the library's main entrance closes at 5 p.m. on weekends, so for evening sessions, use the side door on Oak Street. Any questions so far?

title: Bristol Food and Drink Festival
passage: Good evening, everyone. Welcome to this month's meeting of the Harbourside Community Association. I'm Rachel, the events coordinator, and I'm here to tell you about this year's Bristol Food and Drink Festival. Now in its fifteenth year, the festival will run from Friday the twelfth to Sunday the fourteenth of July, and for the first time it will take place in Queen Square rather than the old dockside site. The reason for the move is simple: we've simply outgrown the docks. Last year we had over sixty stalls, and this year we're expecting closer to ninety, including twelve dedicated to street food from around the world. Entry is free, but please note that the Saturday evening concert with the local jazz band is ticketed, at eight pounds for adults and four for children under twelve. Because the square is surrounded by residential streets, we strongly encourage visitors to use the park-and-ride service from Temple Meads station, which runs every fifteen minutes. And a quick word about volunteering: we still need about thirty helpers to set up on Thursday and to manage the recycling stations over the weekend. If you're interested, please sign up at the back of the hall before you leave tonight. Right, now let me hand over to Tom, who'll tell you about the cooking demonstrations.

title: Welcome to Willow Creek Farmhouse
passage:
Hello everyone, and welcome to Willow Creek Farmhouse. I'm your host, Emma, and I'm delighted to have you here for the weekend. Before you settle in, let me give you a quick tour of the property and explain a few practical details.

First, the farmhouse itself dates back to 1892 and was originally a dairy farm. We restored it five years ago, keeping the original oak beams and stone walls. You'll find your rooms on the first floor. Each room has a kettle, tea and coffee, and a small fridge. The bathrooms are shared, but there are two on each floor, so it's rarely a problem.

Breakfast is served in the conservatory from 7:30 to 9:30. We use eggs from our own hens and bread from the village bakery. If you have any dietary requirements, please let me know tonight so I can plan ahead.

One important thing: we don't have Wi-Fi in the rooms. We do have a strong signal in the main lounge, and many guests actually enjoy the digital detox. There's a wood-burning stove there, and it's a lovely spot to read.

Finally, about the area. There are three walking trails starting from the back gate. The shortest one takes about 40 minutes and leads to a waterfall. The other two are longer and more challenging. Maps are in the hallway. Oh, and please don't feed the chickens — they're on a special diet. Any questions so far?

title: Alpine Ski Resort Safety Announcement
passage: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Pine Ridge Ski Resort. I'm Jamie, your slope safety officer, and I'd like to go over a few important points before you head out to the slopes. First, please note that all skiers and snowboarders must wear helmets. We have rental helmets available at the equipment hut near the main lift, and they're free of charge with any ski pass. Second, our resort has four main runs: Green Circle for beginners, Blue Square for intermediate, and Black Diamond and Double Black Diamond for experts. Please choose a run that matches your ability level. Also, be aware that the upper mountain lifts close at 3:30 PM sharp, so plan your last run accordingly. The lower lifts run until 5:00 PM. One more thing: every Saturday at 2 PM, we offer a free guided mountain tour for intermediate and advanced skiers. You can sign up at the information desk. Finally, if you witness an accident, please do not move the injured person. Instead, call the ski patrol at extension 444 from any resort phone. Our patrol team will respond within minutes. Thank you, and enjoy your day on the mountain!

passage: Hello everyone, and welcome to the City Art Museum. I'm Sarah, your guide for today. Before we start the tour, let me give you some practical information. The museum is open from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., but the last entry is at 5:30. We have three floors. On the ground floor, you'll find the main reception, the gift shop, and a café. The first floor houses our permanent collection of European paintings, and the second floor is currently hosting a special exhibition on ancient Chinese ceramics. That exhibition runs until the end of next month. Please note that photography is allowed in most areas, but flash is not permitted in the special exhibition because it can damage the delicate ceramics. Also, food and drinks are not allowed in the galleries, so please finish your coffee before entering. Now, a few words about the tour. We'll begin with the permanent collection on the first floor, then move to the special exhibition, and finish with a short film about the museum's history in the auditorium on the ground floor. The tour lasts about 90 minutes. If you have any questions during the tour, please feel free to ask. And if you get separated from the group, just meet us at the café at 3 p.m. Alright, let's head to the elevator.

title: A Guided Tour of the Willows Community Park
passage:
Hello everyone, and welcome to the Willows Community Park. I'm Sarah, your guide for today's tour. Before we set off, let me give you a quick overview of what this park offers. The park was established in 1985 and covers about 40 acres. It's divided into three main areas: the formal gardens, the sports zone, and the nature reserve.

We'll start with the formal gardens, which are just ahead. These gardens are famous for their rose collection—over 200 varieties. Please remember not to touch the flowers, as some are quite delicate. After that, we'll walk to the sports zone, where you'll see tennis courts, a basketball court, and a children's playground. The playground was recently renovated and now includes a sensory garden for kids with special needs.

Finally, we'll visit the nature reserve at the far end of the park. This area is a protected habitat for several bird species, including the rare blue heron. Because of this, dogs are not allowed in the nature reserve, even on a leash. The reserve also has a small pond and a wooden boardwalk.

Our tour will last about 90 minutes. If you have any questions, feel free to ask as we go. And please stay with the group—the park is large, and it's easy to get lost. Now, let's begin.

title: Managing Stress for Better Sleep
passage:
Good evening, everyone. Thanks for coming to tonight's health talk. I'm Dr. Rachel Kim from the university wellness center. Tonight, I'll focus on something many students struggle with: stress and its impact on sleep.

You know, when you're stressed, your body releases cortisol, a hormone that keeps you alert. That's fine during the day, but if cortisol levels stay high at night, falling asleep becomes really tough. And then the next day, you're tired, you drink more coffee, and the cycle continues.

So what can you do? First, try to keep a consistent sleep schedule, even on weekends. Your body loves routine. Second, avoid screens for at least an hour before bed. The blue light tricks your brain into thinking it's still daytime. Third, and this is key, don't use your bed for studying or watching videos. Let your brain associate the bed with sleep only.

One more thing: if you wake up in the middle of the night and can't fall back asleep within twenty minutes, get up and do something boring, like reading a dull textbook. Don't just lie there worrying. 

I'll be handing out a sleep diary at the end. Try to fill it out for one week and see what patterns you notice. Any questions so far?

title: Volunteer Recruitment at Riverside Nature Reserve
passage: Hello everyone, and welcome to Riverside Nature Reserve. I'm Sarah, the volunteer coordinator. We're delighted you're considering joining our team. As you may know, this 120-hectare reserve is home to over 200 species of birds and rare plants, but we rely heavily on volunteers to keep it thriving. We have three main roles: visitor guides, who lead weekend tours and need good communication skills; conservation assistants, who help with habitat restoration, often on weekdays; and event helpers, who support our seasonal festivals. All volunteers must attend a one-day training session, which we hold on the first Saturday of each month. No prior experience is needed—just enthusiasm and a minimum commitment of four hours per month. You'll receive a free uniform, a 20% discount at the café, and travel expenses up to ten pounds per day. Now, some of you might be wondering about age limits. We welcome anyone over 16, but under-18s need parental consent. Next, let me explain how to apply. You can pick up an application form from the visitor centre, or download it from our website. The deadline for the autumn intake is September 30th. After that, we'll invite you to a brief informal chat, not a formal interview. So, any questions so far?

title: Welcome to the City Art Gallery's New Exhibition
passage: Hello everyone, and welcome to the City Art Gallery. I'm Emma, your guide for today. Before we begin, let me give you a quick overview of our new exhibition, 'Colours of the North'. title: School Open Day Welcome Talk
passage:
Hello everyone, and welcome to Greenwood Secondary College's annual Open Day. I'm Sarah Mitchell, the Deputy Principal, and I'm delighted to see so many prospective students and families here today.

Before you explore the campus, let me give you a quick overview of what's happening. We have three guided tours running throughout the morning: the first starts at 10 a.m., the second at 11:15, and the last at 12:30. Each tour lasts about 45 minutes and covers the main teaching buildings, the library, and the sports centre.

If you're interested in our music program, don't miss the concert in the auditorium at 11 o'clock, where our senior orchestra will perform. For those curious about science, there's a hands-on experiment session in the science labs from 10:30 to 12:00. Parents who want to discuss enrolment should head to the administration office on the ground floor; staff will be available all day.

One important note: the cafeteria is closed for renovations, so lunch will be served in the gymnasium instead. Free tea and coffee are available there from 10 a.m. onwards.

Finally, please pick up a feedback form at the entrance desk before you leave. Your comments help us improve future events. Enjoy your visit!

title: Road Closure and Bus Route Changes
passage:
Hello, this is a recorded message from the City Transport Authority. I'm calling to inform you about some important changes to bus services in the city centre starting next Monday, the 15th of March. Due to major roadworks on High Street, all buses that normally use that route will be diverted. This includes the Number 10, 22, and 45 services. The work is expected to last for six weeks, so please plan your journeys accordingly. 

Now, here are the details. The Number 10 bus, which usually goes along High Street, will instead turn left at the library and go down Mill Road. It will then rejoin its normal route at the train station. The Number 22 will follow a similar diversion but will stop at the market square instead of the train station. The Number 45 is a bit different. It will avoid the city centre entirely and use the ring road. This means it will not serve the university or the hospital. Passengers for those destinations should take the Number 10 or 22 and change at the station. 

We apologise for any inconvenience. For more information, visit our website or call our helpline. Thank you for listening.

title: Evening Coding Bootcamp Orientation
passage:
Hello everyone, and welcome to the orientation for our evening coding bootcamp. My name is Daniel Reeves, and I'm the program coordinator here at Northgate Community College.

This twelve-week course is designed for complete beginners who want to move into entry-level web development. You don't need any prior programming experience, but you do need to be comfortable using a computer.

Classes run on Tuesday and Thursday evenings from six thirty to nine. That gives us two and a half hours per session, which is longer than most evening courses, but we've found it's necessary because we spend the first forty-five minutes on live coding practice, and the rest on new material.

Now, attendance is not strictly mandatory, but I have to be honest with you: students who miss more than three sessions almost never pass the final project. So please treat it seriously.

One important thing: there's no written exam at the end. Instead, you'll build a small website on your own and present it in the final week. We've found this gives employers a much better idea of what you can actually do.

About materials: all the course notes and video recordings will be posted online every Friday. You don't need to buy any textbooks. But you will need your own laptop — the college computers are only available until five, so they won't help you in the evenings.

Finally, the course fee is nine hundred dollars, and payment plans are available. If you have any questions, please see me after this session.

passage: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the Westside Community Centre. I'm Emma, the coordinator for our adult evening classes. title: The History of the City of Bath
passage: Welcome to the city of Bath. I'm your guide, and today I'll tell you about its fascinating history. Bath is famous for its natural hot springs, which have been used for thousands of years. The Romans built a grand temple and bathing complex here around 60 AD, and they called the town Aquae Sulis. After the Romans left, the baths fell into disrepair, but in the 18th century, the city became a popular spa resort again, thanks to the efforts of Beau Nash, who was a master of ceremonies. He organized social events and made Bath a fashionable place to see and be seen. Many grand Georgian buildings were constructed during this period, such as the Royal Crescent and the Circus. In the 19th century, Bath's popularity declined as people began to prefer seaside resorts. However, in the 20th century, the city was recognized for its historical significance, and in 1987, it was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Today, you can still visit the Roman baths and the Pump Room, where you can taste the mineral water. So let's begin our tour.

title: A Talk at the Science Museum
passage: Hello, and welcome to the City Science Museum. I'm Sarah, your guide for today. Before we start, let me give you a quick overview of what's here. The museum is divided into three main sections: the Space Zone, the Robot Zone, and the Ocean Zone. The Space Zone is on the ground floor, right next to the entrance. You'll find a real moon rock there, and a simulator that lets you experience zero gravity. The Robot Zone is on the first floor. It features robots from the 1980s to the present day. You can even program a robot to draw a picture. The Ocean Zone is in the basement. It has a huge tank with live fish, and a submarine model you can climb inside. One important thing: the museum is closing early today at 3 p.m. for a private event. So please make sure you've seen everything you want to by 2:30. Also, the café on the second floor is closed today, but there's a small coffee cart near the main entrance. Finally, photography is allowed everywhere except in the Ocean Zone, because the flash can harm the fish. If you have any questions, feel free to ask me as we go along. Let's begin our tour.
